articles.summary: 'Bei tempi prima del Reverendo Jones'. Un partito di Di Battista? 'Gli darei una mano'
articles.preview: L'ingresso nello studio di 'Che Tempo che fa' è di quelli che ti aspetti da Beppe Grillo 'non mi applaudite sulla fiducia se non sapete cosa dico". articles.body:
L'ingresso nello studio di 'Che Tempo che fa' è di quelli che ti aspetti da Beppe Grillo 'non mi applaudite sulla fiducia se non sapete cosa dico". Ed è subito show, l'intervento dell'ex garante del Movimento Cinque Stelle.

Grillo è un fiume in piena, passa dai ricordi personali come l'amicizia con Gino Paoli e Renzo Piano, ma non risparmia frecciate a Giuseppe Conte, mai citato se non con l'appellativo 'reverendo Jones' a cui manda però un avviso: "A gennaio ci sarà forse un giudice che dirà che questo simbolo è mio. Io sono sempre in politica, anche quando fai la spesa fai politica, quando scegli il bus. Non sono mai uscito. Se il giudice dice che il Movimento è mio me lo prendo e magari lo darò in uso ai minori di 25 anni".

Insomma nessuna intenzione di farsi da parte, anzi, seppur riconoscendo di non essere più "l'elevato. Ormai sono in una parabola discendete e mi fanno pagare anche il caffè", il comico genovese fa capire di essere pienamente in campo. "Io ci sono, sono l'unico che può cambiare questo Paese, ho una visione diversa", mette in chiaro aggiungendo: "Stiamo rappezzando un cadavere, abbiamo una democrazia che non evolve, l'intelligenza artificiale evolve". E ancora "Non ho più niente da perdere, mi sono impoverito per voi, brutti disgraziati". Poi, parlando del presente: "La pena ti insegue come nei processi papali, non finisce più. Siamo in un momento strano. Si può cambiare questa democrazia, vorrei togliere ciò che c'è in mezzo fra Repubblica e Comuni, fare città Stato. Firenze ha diritto di legiferare nella sua città, fare le tasse, investire nei territori. Servono distretti comunali e togli 150 mila enti inutili. Il Movimento è nato dalla democrazia dal basso, si poteva scegliere dal basso".

Ed è proprio ad un ex big del Movimento, Alessandro Di Battista, quello a cui Grillo guarda. Se facesse un partito "gli darei una mano domani mattina. E' il mio fratello minore".

Parole tenere anche per Luigi Di Maio "era il più bravo di tutti - dice - ora fa il diplomatico, sono orgoglioso. Gli voglio bene a queste persone - ammette - solo che adesso non so dov'è Luigi, credo che viva in un bidone di petrolio, quando si alza il prezzo lui esce. Sono amici d'infanzia. Io ci sono. Se faccio non è per portare via dei voti al campo largo, ma per dare una cosa a ragazzi di 25 anni, sono il padre nobile".

Spazio poi ad uno dei cavalli di battaglia: il nucleare. l'ex garante M5s non ha dubbi: "Non ne abbiamo bisogno, poi dicono che fra 25 anni la bolletta cala, è una presa per il culo.

Bisogna che vi svegliate un attimo". Infine, Grillo si congeda dal pubblico con un saluto che suona più come un arrivederci a molto presto: "Io non me ne vado - avvisa - non me ne sono mai andato perché sono sempre stato qui".

articles.title: Il piano di William, 'Harry potrebbe perdere il titolo di principe'
articles.summary: Il futuro sovrano lavora a una radicale riforma delle regole della casa reale
articles.preview: Una radicale ristrutturazione della monarchia britannica. Il principe William, futuro erede al trono di San Giacomo, figlio di re Carlo III e della defunta principessa Diana, starebbe progettando un piano che priverebbe il fratello Harry, con cui i rapporti sono tesi, del titolo di "principe". La "massiccia ristrutturazione" che l'ex allievo di Eton avrebbe iniziato a elaborare riguarderebbe tutti i membri della famiglia reale che non svolgono attività lavorative, ai quali verrebbe tolto il titolo di Sua Altezza Reale.
articles.body:
Una radicale ristrutturazione della monarchia britannica. Il principe William, futuro erede al trono di San Giacomo, figlio di re Carlo III e della defunta principessa Diana, starebbe progettando un piano che priverebbe il fratello Harry, con cui i rapporti sono tesi, del titolo di "principe". La "massiccia ristrutturazione" che l'ex allievo di Eton avrebbe iniziato a elaborare riguarderebbe tutti i membri della famiglia reale che non svolgono attività lavorative, ai quali verrebbe tolto il titolo di Sua Altezza Reale.

La rivelazione giunge da Tom Sykes, un'autorità in materia, che nel suo prossimo libro in uscita a febbraio, ha messo nero su bianco quella che potrebbe essere la futura casa reale britannica negli anni a venire. Il disegno sarebbe maturato da tempo, considerato che circa anno fa lo stesso William aveva chiarito che non avrebbe avuto paura di prendere decisioni difficili una volta diventato re, annunciando che "il cambiamento è in programma".

Secondo alcune fonti, un elemento centrale dei piani del principe di Galles è garantire che i titoli reali e l'uso di "Sua Altezza Reale" siano più simili a "titoli professionali" che a un privilegio automatico di nascita per i membri più anziani della famiglia. Tuttavia, privare Harry, la moglie Meghan e i loro figli - il principe Archie di 7 anni e la principessa Lilibet di 5 - dei titoli e degli appellativi reali potrebbe acuire drasticamente la frattura tra i due fratelli.

Le potenziali modifiche, però, implicherebbero anche che due dei figli di William e Kate, la principessa Charlotte, di 11 anni, e il principe Louis, di 8, potrebbero rinunciare ai loro titoli e all'uso di Sua Altezza Reale, se, una volta adulti, decidessero di intraprendere carriere indipendenti. In pratica, significherebbe che verrebbe loro offerta la possibilità di scegliere se servire o meno come "riserve" della Corona. Ciò non avrebbe però ripercussioni sul principe George, il cui futuro, in quanto erede al trono, è, a quanto si afferma, "già segnato".

A divulgare in anteprima le indiscrezioni è stato il Daily Mail, da sempre attento alle vicende reali, precisando che, come da prassi, da Kensington Palace non è giunto alcun commento in proposito. Secondo l'autore del testo coloro che gravitano intorno a William credono che una riforma di questo tipo potrebbe sicuramente ottenere "un enorme sostegno pubblico in un Paese sempre più insofferente ai costi e agli eccessi percepiti di una casa reale così estesa".

Inoltre, si sostiene, che tale piano sia stato concepito per evitare il ripetersi delle imbarazzanti controversie che hanno coinvolto il principe Harry e soprattutto Andrea Mountbatten-Windsor, figlio terzogenito della regina Elisabetta privato di tutti i suoi titoli in seguito allo scandalo delle frequentazioni con Jeffrey Epstein. Il tabloid britannico rivela inoltre che William starebbe già crescendo i suoi tre figli lontani da alcuni degli orpelli formali del loro status reale.

Stando ad alcune fonti, né gli assistenti né il personale di casa li chiamerebbero "Sua Altezza Reale", e a scuola non ci si rivolge loro appellandoli principe o principessa. George verrebbe indicato semplicemente come George Wales quando Eton pubblica i risultati e gli eventi sportivi. Non era così per suo padre William, che quando frequentava la scuola nei resoconti sportivi veniva chiamato "Principe William".

articles.summary: AGI - Patrimoniale , la tassa sui grandi patrimoni scava un solco fra la segretaria del Pd , Elly Schlein , e gli alleati di Avs . Tra le due parti "ballano" 95 milioni di euro: la differenza tra la tassa ai super ricchi alla quale pensano i rossoverdi, sui patrimoni a partire da 5,4 milioni di euro, e quella di cui parla la leader dem da Parigi. Una tassa che vada a incidere per il 2 per cento sui patrimoni da 100 milioni di euro. Schlein da Parigi: la proposta Zucman "Tassare del 2% all'anno chi ha più di 100 milioni di euro? Appoggiamo la proposta di Zucman , è quella che portiamo al tavolo della discussione con i nostri alleati progressisti", annuncia la dem dal Paris Summit Against International Oligarchy , al Theatre de la Concorde . "Una tassazione minima del 2 per cento a chi ha più di 100 milioni di euro non deve fare paura. Noi non tasseremo il ceto medio, a differenza del governo Meloni che ha portato la pressione fiscale al record degli ultimi 12 anni. È una proposta equa che riguarda la giustizia". Poco prima, Schlein aveva parlato di una norma a livello globale, come fatto già in passato quando, davanti alla proposta di Nicola Fratoianni , rispose di essere pronta, qualora si trattasse di una norma a livello europeo. Patrimoniale, Fratoianni avverte e Conte frena "Senza patrimoniale non c'è coalizione", ha avvertito pochi giorni fa Fratoianni rispondendo a chi gli chiedeva dei dubbi sollevati da Giuseppe Conte : il leader del M5s considera un errore introdurre una patrimoniale sui grandi patrimoni in Italia: il rischio sarebbe di fare fuggire gli investimenti dal nostro Paese. Da Avs , però, rispondono che il timore è infondato, "lo dicono molti studi". E poi, si sorride in casa rossoverde, la exit tax del governo ci ha spianato la strada. Ironia che maschera il nervosismo per un confronto che si va avvitando. Campo largo diviso anche sul sostegno a Kiev E non solo sulla patrimoniale. Il tavolo Esteri del cantiere del programma è stato nuovamente aggiornato, questa volta a martedì prossimo, nell'impossibilità di arrivare a dama sul tema del sostegno a Kiev . I rappresentanti della coalizione si vedranno, questa volta, in presenza. Ma, riferiscono fonti presenti al tavolo, si fa sempre più concreta l'ipotesi che a sciogliere il nodo del sostegno all'Ucraina possano essere i leader dei partiti. Il Movimento 5 Stelle e Avs rimangono sulla linea dello stop all'invio di armamenti a Kiev. I centristi di Italia Viva e Più Europa non vogliono deflettere dall'aiuto con ogni mezzo al popolo ucraino. Il Pd è più cauto e cerca la formula capace di tenere insieme le diverse sensibilità. Ma sembra difficile che possa passare l'idea, già sul tavolo, di sostituire l'invio di armi con l'invio di materiali civili. "Lasciamo lavorare i tavoli, ma io sono fiduciosa che lavoreremo per trovare una sintesi alta su tutti i temi e che presto riusciremo insieme a interpretare una sfida elettorale fondamentale non solo per il futuro del Paese ma anche per il futuro dell'Europa", dice la segretaria dem.

articles.title: Borse di studio sospese agli studenti indagati, polemiche sull'emendamento Delmastro
articles.summary: AGI - " Revoca dei benefici nell'ambito del diritto allo studio ". È il titolo dell'emendamento presentato dal deputato di Fratelli d'Italia Andrea Delmastro al decreto scuola. Una proposta che innesca la reazione delle opposizioni: "Impunità per gli amici, repressione per studenti e lavoratori che protestano", è il commento di Giuseppe Conte. Nel dettaglio, è l'emendamento 5.020, firmato proprio da Delmastro, quello su cui si concentra l'ira del centrosinistra. Prevede che "benefici economici, contributi, borse di studio, provvidenze e ogni altra utilità comunque riconosciuti nell'ambito del diritto allo studio sono sospesi nei confronti dello studente che risulti sottoposto a indagini preliminari per uno dei delitti di cui agli articoli 336, 337, 339, 419, 420, 421, 421-bis, 582, 583 e 635 del codice penale, commessi nel corso o in occasione di manifestazioni, proteste od occupazioni, fino alla definizione del procedimento penale", si legge nel testo dell'emendamento. "Il Pubblico Ministero deve informare senza ritardo l'amministrazione che eroga il beneficio", scuola o università, "dell'iscrizione della notizia di reato". In caso di condanna, è prevista "la revoca del beneficio, con possibilità di restituzione in tutto o in parte delle somme già erogate per il periodo in cui si sono verificati i fatti. Nei casi di particolare gravità: esclusione dall'accesso ai benefici del diritto allo studio per i due anni accademici o scolastici successivi". Conte: "Basta un'accusa per perdere la borsa di studio" Per Conte, "sono le nuove frontiere della loro idea di sicurezza: colpire il diritto allo studio, intimidire chi manifesta, trasformare il dissenso in una colpa da sanzionare". Il leader del Movimento 5 Stelle si sofferma sul fatto che "tra i protagonisti di questa stretta c'è Andrea Delmastro. Proprio lui. Lo stesso Delmastro che ha beneficiato dello scudo parlamentare per negare alla Procura di Roma l'autorizzazione ad acquisire le chat con un prestanome della Camorra sugli affari in comune tramite una società di ristorazione", sottolinea Conte, che rincara: per gli studenti "basta un'accusa per perdere la borsa di studio. Delmastro e i fedelissimi di Meloni possono invece usare il Parlamento per scudarsi". Da qui la richiesta indirizzata alla presidente del Consiglio: "Cara Giorgia Meloni, se vuoi togliere benefici a indagati, inquisiti e condannati, non perdere tempo a cercarli nelle scuole e nelle università. Guarda dentro il tuo partito. Comincia dai tuoi sodali. Comincia da chi chiede repressione per gli studenti e pretende immunità per sé". Schlein: "Le borse di studio garantiscono maggiori opportunità" Per Elly Schlein l'emendamento di FdI si inserisce in quelle politiche con cui "le destre nel mondo hanno ucciso la speranza di un domani dignitoso alle giovani generazioni che ora protestano". "Ai giovani", continua la leader del Pd, "le borse di studio sono proprio quello strumento che ai giovani garantisce maggiori opportunità in un mondo sempre più diseguale. La destra dovrebbe interrogarsi sulle ragioni della protesta, anziché cercare nuovi strumenti per scoraggiarla". Grimaldi (Avs): "Delmastro garantista solo per le sue chat" Il vicecapogruppo di Avs alla Camera, Marco Grimaldi, attacca frontalmente Delmastro: "Pensa di fare il duro con i ragazzi, ma è garantista solo per le sue chat. È lo stesso che da sottosegretario alla Giustizia per dossieraggio contro le opposizioni ha passato a Donzelli i colloqui dal carcere di Sassari tra Cospito e gli altri detenuti al 41-bis, ed è stato condannato in primo grado a 8 mesi per rivelazione di segreto d'ufficio. È lo stesso che era socio al 25% della Bisteccheria d'Italia, amministrata da una diciottenne figlia di Mauro Caroccia, condannato in via definitiva per intestazione fittizia aggravata dal metodo mafioso, per vicende legate al clan dei Senese". Bonelli: "Si vuole punire chi protesta" E il leader rossoverde Angelo Bonelli chiosa: "Gli emendamenti di FdI sono roba da squallido regime. Un milione e mezzo di persone scende in piazza contro il carovita e il giorno dopo Fratelli d'Italia risponde con 27 emendamenti che hanno un solo obiettivo: punire chi protesta e spaventare chi vorrebbe farlo. È la logica di chi non tollera il dissenso e lo tratta come un reato".

articles.title: Non si sa come il “campo largo” voglia ripristinare il reddito di cittadinanza
articles.summary: I partiti di centrosinistra hanno raggiunto un accordo, ma restano da chiarire i destinatari della misura e le coperture economiche
articles.preview: Il 19 novembre diverse fonti stampa hanno dato la notizia secondo cui i partiti del “campo largo” avrebbero raggiunto un’intesa per inserire il ripristino del reddito di cittadinanza nel programma per le prossime elezioni politiche, previste nel 2027. Il “campo largo” è il nome con cui viene chiamata nel gergo giornalistico l’alleanza di centrosinistra formata da Partito Democratico, Movimento 5 Stelle e Alleanza Verdi-Sinistra, a cui si sono uniti di recente Italia Viva, Più Europa e Più Uno, il nuovo soggetto politico dell’ex direttore dell’Agenzia…
articles.body:
Il 19 novembre diverse fonti stampa hanno dato la notizia secondo cui i partiti del “campo largo” avrebbero raggiunto un’intesa per inserire il ripristino del reddito di cittadinanza nel programma per le prossime elezioni politiche, previste nel 2027. Il “campo largo” è il nome con cui viene chiamata nel gergo giornalistico l’alleanza di centrosinistra formata da Partito Democratico, Movimento 5 Stelle e Alleanza Verdi-Sinistra, a cui si sono uniti di recente Italia Viva, Più Europa e Più Uno, il nuovo soggetto politico dell’ex direttore dell’Agenzia delle entrate Ernesto Maria Ruffini.

Il tavolo della coalizione dedicato al lavoro ha dato il via libera a un testo condiviso sul “reddito minimo garantito”, la misura che entrerà nel programma comune in vista delle elezioni del 2027. La nuova denominazione richiama la raccomandazione del Consiglio dell’Unione europea del 30 gennaio 2023 sull’adeguatezza del reddito minimo e l’inclusione attiva, ma non è ancora chiaro nel dettaglio come funzionerebbe la misura.

Se da una parte i partiti del centrosinistra sembrano concordare sulla necessità di uno strumento più ampio per sostenere le persone in povertà, dall’altra restano da definire la platea dei beneficiari, i requisiti per accedere al sostegno e le risorse necessarie per finanziarlo.

Venerdì 20 novembre, in un centinaio di piazze italiane, lavoratori e studenti hanno manifestato per chiedere salari più alti, sicurezza sul lavoro e maggiori investimenti nei servizi pubblici. Con questo sciopero generale, proclamato dalla CGIL per protestare contro le politiche economiche del governo Meloni, si contano nove scioperi generali nazionali da inizio anno. E secondo il calendario della Commissione di garanzia sugli scioperi, altri due sono in programma per il prossimo 4 dicembre. Ma quanti scioperi generali si sono svolti negli ultimi dieci anni? E qual è il governo sotto cui ne sono stati effettuati di più?

In breve, il governo Meloni è quello durante il quale si è svolto il maggior numero di scioperi generali nazionali, ma se si tiene conto della durata dei governi la classifica cambia. A seconda dell’esecutivo infatti si va da una media di uno sciopero generale ogni poco più di due settimane a uno ogni oltre tre mesi. E il governo Draghi è in testa a questa classifica.

articles.body:
Come ogni anno in questo periodo, fa discutere la grande quantità di emendamenti presentati dai parlamentari al disegno di legge di Bilancio. Lo scorso 17 novembre è scaduto il termine per la presentazione degli emendamenti alla manovra per il 2027 in Commissione Bilancio alla Camera. Secondo fonti stampa, i vari gruppi parlamentari presenti alla Camera hanno presentato circa 6.600 proposte di modifica al testo.

Abbiamo verificato e si tratta del numero più alto di emendamenti presentati in prima lettura a un disegno di legge di Bilancio nel corso di questa legislatura. L’anno scorso, in occasione del primo esame della manovra al Senato, erano stati 5.700, nel 2024 circa 4.500, nel 2023 3.300, mentre nel 2022 erano stati 3 mila. Quello di quest’anno non è comunque un primato dell’ultimo decennio: nel 2021, durante l’esame della legge di Bilancio per il 2022, approvata durante il governo Draghi, in Commissione Bilancio al Senato erano state presentate quasi 7.500 proposte di modifica. Nel complesso, secondo le nostre verifiche, dal 2016 a oggi i parlamentari hanno presentato quasi 60 mila emendamenti alla manovra, con una media di circa 6 mila emendamenti per ogni legge di Bilancio. Per calcolare il totale degli emendamenti abbiamo considerato quelli presentati nel primo ramo del Parlamento in cui viene esaminata la manovra, visto che di solito solo la prima camera riesce a modificare il disegno di legge di Bilancio.

articles.title: Questo video di Ronaldo al Pallone d’Oro con la bandiera della Palestina è falso
articles.summary: Il calciatore portoghese non era presente alla cerimonia del 2026, e nella scena ci sono diversi errori tipici dei programmi di IA generativa
articles.preview: Il 18 novembre 2026 su X è stato condiviso un video di Cristiano Ronaldo sul red carpet della cerimonia del Pallone d’Oro, uno dei più prestigiosi premi calcistici, mentra indossa la bandiera della Palestina e urla in spagnolo «Palestina libre, que vive Palestina» (ovvero, «Palestina libera, viva la Palestina»). Per questo, Ronaldo viene portato via da due agenti della polizia. L’autore del post applaude il comportamento di Ronaldo, definendolo «MITICOOO». È un video creato con l’intelligenza artificiale, che diffonde una notizia falsa.
articles.body:
Il 18 novembre 2026 su X è stato condiviso un video di Cristiano Ronaldo sul red carpet della cerimonia del Pallone d’Oro, uno dei più prestigiosi premi calcistici, mentra indossa la bandiera della Palestina e urla in spagnolo «Palestina libre, que vive Palestina» (ovvero, «Palestina libera, viva la Palestina»). Per questo, Ronaldo viene portato via da due agenti della polizia.

L’autore del post applaude il comportamento di Ronaldo, definendolo «MITICOOO».

È un video creato con l’intelligenza artificiale, che diffonde una notizia falsa.

Nessun media ha riportato la presunta notizia del calciatore portoghese portato via dalle forze dell’ordine durante la cerimonia di assegnazione del Pallone d’Oro, tenutasi il 26 ottobre 2026 al Palladium Theatre di Londra, per aver espresso solidarietà alla Palestina. Tra l’altro, Ronaldo non era presente alla cerimonia.

Il video infatti è stato creato con un programma di intelligenza artificiale generativa, come si può notare da alcuni dettagli che non corrispondono alla realtà e da alcuni errori nella scena. Ad esempio, nel backdrop del red carpet reale erano disegnati anche i loghi degli sponsor, e non solo del Pallone d’Oro (come si vede invece nel video falso), e i fotografi sullo sfondo non erano posizionati sotto al backdrop, ma di fronte, oltre il red carpet. Tra l’altro, le figure dei fotografi sono indistinguibili tra di loro, e restano immobili per tutto il filmato.

A pubblicare originariamente il contenuto IA è stato, il 13 novembre 2026, l’account TikTok “Cristiano Ronaldo fans” (@zazahamza32) che pubblica esclusivamente deepfake del calciatore portoghese in sostegno della Palestina, come specificato in biografia.

Sul video TikTok è presente il watermark di Sora – il generatore di video IA di OpenAI – una piccola nuvoletta animata con gli occhi e la scritta “Sora”, che contrassegna la natura artificiale della scena. Il video in analisi è stato dunque editato per evitare che si vedesse il watermark.

Pauline Hanson says One Nation has ‘set the agenda for the Liberal party’

One Nation’s Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce are also out the front of Parliament House.

They may have shared a stage with Taylor and Canavan but they’re certainly not being friendly.

Hanson accuses the Coalition and Labor of being a “uni” party (could have come up with a better name there in my opinion) and that they’ve both led the country “to its demise”.

We have been [the ones] that have set the agenda for the Liberal party. They gave up the ghost. They’ve agreed with the uni party in here, and they are the uni party. They’ve, you know, supported each other on the policies that have led this country to the demise that it is in now.

Hanson talks about how she backs small businesses and that two-thirds of her party are small business owners.

Hanson, for reference, has said she wants to make it easier for businesses, particularly small businesses, to fire their workers, and pushed back against wage rises for minimum wage workers.

Labor considering Greens’ amendments on digital duty of care

Anika Wells says the government is considering the Greens’ amendments to the digital duty of care bill (DDOC), including allowing Australians to directly sue big tech companies, and increased financial penalties.

Labor wants the DDOC through parliament this week and Guardian Australia understands the government and the Greens are keen to make a deal. But the Greens aren’t ready to back it yet, holding out for stronger legislation.

A Labor-chaired Senate report on Friday recommended the government amend its own bill to allow a private right of action. In a news conference this morning, the communications minister said she had been “speaking a lot across the weekend” with her Greens counterpart, Sarah Hanson-Young, and indicated things were moving. Wells said:

We’re working through what [private right of action] might look like, as well as the request for amendments on revenue as a penalty. We understand the argument.

We’ve got a lot of considerations to settle and I look forward to both negotiating with parliamentarians and with the cabinet to try and secure something that delivers Australia a basic safety standard in an industry that has been the wild west for far too long.

Wells was critical that the Coalition had “benched themselves” in this discussion, with the Liberal communications spokesperson, Sarah Henderson, having consistently said she wouldn’t back the bill. Wells said:

I find it baffling when online safety and the safety of our kids, the mental welfare of our kids, is one of the most compelling and pressing policy questions of the generation. To bench themselves on this topic is for [the Coalition] to explain.

In pics: Liberals, Nationals and One Nation appear at rally against tax changes

Angus Taylor, a group of his Coalition MPs, and One Nation were out the front of parliament earlier addressing a rally against the government’s capital gains tax changes.

Taylor promised he would reverse them if elected (something he’s said previously).

The political contingency probably made up about 10-20% of everyone there. I’m told there were about 50ish attendees.

Independent pushes government to publish ministerial diaries

Independent MP Monique Ryan has introduced a bill this morning that would force ministers to regularly publish their diaries.

She told a news conference earlier that her constituents were sick of seeing a government they said was not acting in the interests of the public on issues such as gambling and gas.

They’d [constituents] like to know who our ministers meet with, when, where and why. They’re incredibly frustrated that a government that claimed before it was elected that it would be transparent and open has been so manifestly opaque.

Ryan said she had put in a freedom of information request for attorney general, Michelle Rowland’s diary. When she received it, 45% was redacted.

The government is extremely unlikely to support the bill.

Pauline Hanson says One Nation has ‘set the agenda for the Liberal party’

One Nation’s Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce are also out the front of Parliament House.

They may have shared a stage with Taylor and Canavan but they’re certainly not being friendly.

Hanson accuses the Coalition and Labor of being a “uni” party (could have come up with a better name there in my opinion) and that they’ve both led the country “to its demise”.

We have been [the ones] that have set the agenda for the Liberal party. They gave up the ghost. They’ve agreed with the uni party in here, and they are the uni party. They’ve, you know, supported each other on the policies that have led this country to the demise that it is in now.

Hanson talks about how she backs small businesses and that two-thirds of her party are small business owners.

Hanson, for reference, has said she wants to make it easier for businesses, particularly small businesses, to fire their workers, and pushed back against wage rises for minimum wage workers.

Taylor and Canavan appear with Joseph Daoud outside parliament

Joseph Daoud, the man who won an auction to play tennis against the prime minister so he could criticise reforms to the capital gains tax, is back lobbying against the reforms.

Daoud formed “Stop the Ambition Tax”, a self-proclaimed grassroots movement of small business owners against the CGT changes, which is campaigning out the front of Parliament House today.

The Liberal leader, Angus Taylor, and the Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, are appearing with Daoud out the front of parliament too.

Canavan makes some claims that the CGT changes are just the start for “socialists” who supposedly want to control everyone. It’s a stretch to say the least … Canavan must have been doing some yoga this morning.

This is not just about taxes, it’s not just about a budget strategy. This is socialism, ladies and gentlemen. That’s what they are. They are socialists. And they want to control you.

The address becomes a bit of a press conference with Taylor then turning his attention to Cop.

He says it’s the second “flop” for the government after the failed Indigenous voice referendum.

This is the second major flop from this government. This effectively, this climate change Cop flop is [the voice] 2.0. The government has now spent half a billion dollars on two major initiatives that have delivered absolutely nothing but division and hopelessness for the Australian people.

The shadow energy minister, Dan Tehan, isn’t pulling punches on the failure of the Cop climate summit to reach agreement on a deal.

“Chris Bowen must resign today,” Tehan said in a statement.

As the lead negotiator, Chris Bowen is personally responsible for this catastrophic diplomatic disaster.

The Coalition, and Tehan specifically, have consistently poured scorn on Australia’s initial bid to host the conference, and then on Bowen’s installation as president of negotiations. The failure of the summit to reach a consensus is being heralded by the Coalition as vindication of its doubts.

Australian taxpayers have funded Chris Bowen’s $150m Cop pretensions, only for the so-called president to embarrass Australia on the world stage by making jokes about his penis. Of course, the one thing Chris Bowen has not failed to do is spend taxpayers’ money.

If Chris Bowen does not resign immediately, the prime minister should sack him.

Tributes are flowing for Molly Meldrum, the Australian music journalist, broadcaster and producer, who has died at the age of 83. He died in the early hours of Monday morning at a hospital in Melbourne.

On social media, the Liberal leader, Angus Taylor, wrote:

Like so many, I remember watching Molly on Countdown and Hey Hey it’s Saturday. Donning his cowboy hat, Molly became a beloved and recognisable face on Australian television. Kind, gentle and cheerful, Molly’s qualities beamed into our living rooms.

Molly will be dearly missed and fondly remembered as an Australian cultural icon.

The former Nationals leader Michael McCormack wrote on social media “like many young people growing up in that unforgettable decade or so starting in the mid 1970s, I recall sitting in the TV room with my sisters ‘doing ourselves a favour’ watching Countdown hosted by the late, great Ian ‘Molly’ Meldrum. Vale, an Aussie rock music icon.”

Cop breakdown a ‘comprehensive failure’ by Labor, Greens say

The Greens have joined the pile-on against Labor after the Cop climate conference, at which Chris Bowen was a co-president, failed to reach consensus.

The minor party is pretty mad that the government and the proposed deal failed to mention fossil fuels.

The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, told the media:

The prime minister went to a global climate conference and delivered a keynote speech, which failed to mention fossil fuels, and that gave comfort and strength to the fossil fuel industry, who ran that narrative for the whole of Cop31.

At the end of Cop31, we have the Albanese Labor government choosing to side with Saudi Arabia and Trump, and not mention fossil fuels, rather than back in Europe and our Pacific members.

Language and dress standards down in parliament, Hume says

The deputy Liberal leader, Jane Hume, says she can see the standards of behaviour declining in parliament, after a report from my Guardian colleagues that found swearing has drastically increased in the building over the last 20 years.

2026 is the worst year on record for the use of swear words and language deemed “unparliamentary” – and it’s not even over! Take a read of our story here:

Credit where credit is due, Hume’s attire and hair are always impeccable – best blow dry in the parliament, I reckon. She told News24 earlier this morning:

It’s kind of a sad indictment, I think, on the standards of behaviour that we’re beginning to accept in parliament. Look, I reckon there’s a correlation too between, you know, the type of language that we’re seeing, as well as the standard of dress. Our standards of dress has gone down quite dramatically in parliament too.

Australians expect a level of dignity from their representatives. I’m part of the parliamentary standards committee, I think that maybe this is something that was worth considering.

Government ‘limited’ in providing cost of living measures, Albanese says

Keeping PBS medications at $25 to 2030 will cost the budget about $242m, Mark Butler says, but the PM concedes government won’t have room for many more – if any – cost-of-living measures.

We’re counting down to the midyear economic forecast (I mean … at least Jim Chalmers is), where the government has flagged some cost-saving measures as it tries to bring down inflation.

Albanese says:

There’s a limited amount that we can do in terms of cost of living measures … We want to make sure that anything we do makes inflation better, because we know that this is a real challenge. So you will see savings in Myefo; they will be substantial and the treasurer will, of course, be having more to say about that.

Don’t ‘jump at shadows’: Albanese bats off defence bill criticism

Anthony Albanese has tried to bat off concern over a defence bill that critics warn could have serious implications for democracy.

My colleague Sarah Basford Canales explains the situation here:

The long and the short of it is the government, with the support of the Coalition, will pass a bill that will criminalise photographs of defence sites and give security officials the ability to search and detain people suspected of trying to enter designated zones.

The Greens and civil rights groups warn that could capture peaceful protesters and other civilians standing outside defence zones.

Albanese is dismissive of the criticisms:

People shouldn’t jump at shadows, and that is what I’ve seen some of the commentary at doing, reaching absurd proportions. It will be accountable, obviously, for things that are designated, but we live in unsafe times.

I find it remarkable in 2026 as a question over whether we need to designate areas as being protected and we live in times where we know there are more conflicts in the world today than at any time since World War II.

Private health insurance legislation being negotiated in ‘good faith’

Keeping PBS medications to $25 is likely to be a slam dunk for the government – it’s politically easy policy.

A much trickier battle is ahead though, with the government still searching for support to increase private health insurance rebates for over 65s. The Coalition have said there’s no chance they will support that bill.

The health minister, Mark Butler, says the government is negotiating in good faith with the Greens – who want pensioners carved out.

We’re in negotiations with the Greens party. Have been over the last little while and, yes, we would hope to have that legislation dealt with in the Senate this week.

We conduct negotiations under this prime minister in good faith. We listen to the Senate. We understand we don’t have the numbers in the Senate to pass this bill right now in the form that we introduced it. So, of course, we’re negotiating to see what we can achieve.

Albanese announces PBS medication to stay $25 until the end of the decade

Anthony Albanese is back in the country after appearances at international summits in China and the Philippines.

He has called a press conference to announce the government will introduce legislation to keep PBS-listed medication priced at $25 until 2030.

Labor is under significant pressure as the cost of living rises – so the PM is hopeful this will bring some relief to both household purses and his government.

Today we will introduce legislation to extend the freeze of the cost of PBS medicines at just $25 until the end of the decade.

This helps Australians now with the cost of medicines but it helps to keep our nation healthier as well, and we understand the cost of essential medicines can put pressure on household budgets and that’s why we’re giving Australians access to cheaper medicines.

Under the former government, when we came to office, PBS co-payments soared, but now medicines would have cost over $50 per script for general patients.

New nest of red imported fire ants found and destroyed in Sydney

The NSW government discovered a new nest of red imported fire ants in Sydney over the weekend, with findings suggesting the nest could be about a year old.

Officials destroyed the colony, found in Auburn in the city’s west, after it was deemed to contained red imported fire ants, a major invasive species that poses threats to both human health and the environment.

A separate nest was discovered two months ago at the Enfield logistics centre, more than 6km from the site found this weekend. The new nest was found outside a biosecurity control zone and officials are investigating if it is a different infestation originating from another source. Detection dogs are set to be on site soon and a new biosecurity control order is being developed.

Tara Moriarty, the NSW minister for agriculture, said:

Human movement of materials is the primary way fire ants spread, which is why we’re asking everyone to stay alert and report anything suspicious.

Everyone has a part to play in biosecurity, and I thank the member of the public for reporting this site in Auburn.

Coalition wants a gas reservation scheme, says Jane Hume

… But not at “any cost”, Hume says.

The Coalition’s big problem now is that they’re worried the scheme creates an oversupply of gas in the domestic market by design, which would lower gas prices.

They say that could deter new gas investment or even lead to gas slowly dying off.

Hume says the government has already made key concessions by carving out WA, so she’s hopeful there can be a deal.

We want a gas reservation. We’ve been saying that from the start but it can’t be at any price. The government has moved a long way. I think the carveout of WA was a significant move and a good start. But there’s more that can be done.

We want to make sure that we get the calibration of this right. We can’t afford an oversupply domestically that would have detrimental effects on prices for investors. We need new gas in the system, more gas in the system, more investment in gas.

Jane Hume has not missed an opportunity to stick the knife into Chris Bowen after the UN Cop summit failed to reach a consensus after historically long talks.

Sitting in the hot seat after Murray Watt in the RN Breakfast studio, Hume says Bowen failed overseas, while Australians have also faced rising energy prices.

Not only has he failed in these negotiations as the lead negotiator but he’s also failed Australians at the time when he has spent $150m just to be there, just to get this presidency in the first place.

Our energy prices have gone up. Our emissions have flatlined. I think that’s kind of disappointing. He’s really got a job to do at home.

Labor wants gas reservation scheme passed this week

Labor is trying its hand at playing off the Coalition and Greens to get its gas reservation scheme through this week.

The environment minister, Murray Watt, says the Coalition was the party most likely to support the legislation but is now being a bit “intransigent” so Labor could instead make a deal with the Greens.

At face value it looks like a tactic to try to strong-arm the Coalition back to the negotiation table because it’s a policy similar to what they themselves had proposed before the last election under Peter Dutton.

And the government has already made a major concession by carving out WA from the scheme.

Watt says:

I think, up until last week, we certainly felt that the Coalition was the more likely party but we’re seeing the same kind of intransigence from them that we saw last year with the EPBC reforms. But this week is an important week and this is the week that the Coalition can decide if they support cheaper gas. That’s certainly the intention.

I think it’s also worth noting one other group that has evaded scrutiny on this is Pauline Hanson’s One Nation party. They have traditionally supported a gas reservation but, mysteriously, shortly after Gina Rinehart, who’s a big gas producer, has supported their party, they’ve flipped their position.

articles.title: Israel carries out more demolitions in southern Lebanon
articles.summary: Israel carries out more demolitions in southern Lebanon Israeli forces detonated explosives to destroy structures on the outskirts of Qantara in southern Lebanon , Lebanon's National News Agency (NNA) reported. Earlier on Sunday, Israeli forces set off a massive explosion in Zawtar al-Sharqiyah, followed by another in Kfar Tibnit, according to NNA. The blasts could be heard across much of southern Lebanon. Residents of Nabatieh al-Fawqa and Zawtar held two separate protests against the Lebanese government's "silence" over Israel's occupation of areas up to the Litani River, which began in March, according to NNA. Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri said he would not accept congratulations on Lebanon's Independence Day, which falls on 22 November, in solidarity with residents of the occupied southern border villages. In a statement, Berri described this year's independence as "incomplete and unfulfilled". He said it would be complete only once Lebanese territory was liberated and official and popular positions were united again.

Director of U.S. National Intelligence Jay Clayton said that Nvidia Corp. is a perpetual target for people trying to illegally obtain its high-end chips and the U.S. is investigating an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with the company’s former chief executive.

“Nvidia chips, they are the jewel. They are the absolute top that everybody wants,” Clayton said Sunday on ABC’s This Week. “That’s why we’re focusing on this. People will do a lot, they will break the law. There are indictments already involving other companies where people have broken the law to get access to Nvidia chips.”

He said in a separate interview on CNN’s State of the Union that Attorney General Todd Blanche has made it clear that the U.S. is looking into Alice Huang, a former executive for Singapore-based Megaspeed International, and her company but declined to comment further.

articles.title: Can climate diplomacy build on the collapse of COP31?
articles.summary: The failures of this year's talks in Turkey, which follow weak outcomes at earlier COPs, lay bare a need for change.
articles.preview: ANTALYA, Turkey – The collapse of COP31 talks in Turkey on Sunday without a political agreement left exhausted negotiators questioning the future of a process that for three decades has led the global fight against climate change. For the small, vulnerable countries most exposed to rising sea levels and the increasingly extreme weather scientists link to rising carbon emissions, annual U.N. conferences are their chance to draw the world’s attention to their plight and seek financial help.
articles.body:
ANTALYA, Turkey – The collapse of COP31 talks in Turkey on Sunday without a political agreement left exhausted negotiators questioning the future of a process that for three decades has led the global fight against climate change.

For the small, vulnerable countries most exposed to rising sea levels and the increasingly extreme weather scientists link to rising carbon emissions, annual U.N. conferences are their chance to draw the world’s attention to their plight and seek financial help.

But the failure of the Turkish talks, which follows on from weak outcomes at other COPs in recent years, lays bare the need for change.

Andres Martin Garrido Sanchez, director of environment in Peru’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said “the credibility of the process” was at stake.

“This system needs in-depth reforms,” he said.

Simon Stiell, the U.N. climate chief representing the U.N. convention that underpins international climate talks, said the consensus-based system can still function, but work was needed.

“I have taken steps in engaging external knowledge leaders in advising on areas of potential reform. That is something I will be championing with considerable effort as we leave here,” he said as the talks ended on Sunday.

Two stand-out victories for U.N. climate diplomacy were the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, when the world for the first time agreed on legally binding targets to curb climate emissions and the 2015 Paris agreement, which established an aspiration to limit global warming to no more than 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit).

A major difference in Paris compared with Antalya was that the U.S. was still engaged in the climate process in 2015.

The Antalya talks, the first since a U.N. report saying the world was set to breach the 1.5 C threshold that can prevent the worst consequences of warming, marked the second climate conference since U.S. President Donald Trump withdrew from the U.N. climate process.

China, the world’s biggest carbon emitter, but also a major part of the solution as a provider of low-carbon technology, has attended the talks but sought to be low profile.

James Fletcher, who led the CARICOM group of Caribbean nations in Antalya, cited the lack of a major power backing a positive outcome as a big issue.

“There isn’t that one party that has sufficient gravitas that can get parties that may be far apart to come together,” he said.

Delegates said, however, the need for a multilateral deal to direct the shift towards renewable energy has become less necessary as renewable energy becomes economically compelling.

China’s clean energy exports last year alone, for example, will help the Global South avoid 257 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions per year once deployed — an amount equal to the emissions of France, according to analysis by Lauri Myllyvirta, co-founder of the Helsinki-based Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

The business world as a result is less dependent on COPs to guide investment decisions.

“It used to be that you’d worry about how these (COP) decisions might affect the investment signal,” said Chris Dodwell, co-head of the sustainability center at Impax Asset Management.

“I don’t think they really have that impact anymore ... the economics have taken over and are driving the transition.”

And bad as the absence of a deal was, some saw a hint of the positive in the wider refusal to accept a weak deal.

The determination of big oil producers, led by Saudi Arabia, to block language on fossil fuel, arguably reflected the scale of progress that has been achieved.

“The fact that they are blocking so much is also an expression of the fact that we are accelerating the transition,” Mattias Frumerie, Sweden’s chief negotiator, said.

“They’re seeing the direction of travel and this is the forum where they can express their frustration.”

Like-minded governments, meanwhile, have focused on smaller groups to get things done. They have formed alliances to push together for faster emissions cuts and to rally finance, forestry initiatives, and efficiency programs.

Such forums include the Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels, or TAFF, the Green Grids Initiative, the Global Methane Pledge and the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance.

“There is growing interest in how can we work together to move, not through consensus, but through a coalition of people that are willing to work together,” said Maina Talia, climate minister of Tuvalu, which will next year host TAFF. As one of the low-lying Pacific island nations, Tuvalu is particularly keen for rapid action to address climate change.

He said he expected roughly 90 countries to send representatives including Britain, Mexico and Nigeria.

Fiji, another Pacific island, voiced its exasperation with COP.

“It is exhausting and frustrating and disappointing when you come year in, year out and there is no movement,” Lynda Tabuya, Fiji’s climate minister, said.

The country’s chief negotiator, Sivendra Michael, however, said the consensus-driven process of COPs remained vital to ensuring the progress achieved by previous conferences was maintained.

“I do not know how else we are going to bring together all the parties that have committed legally to a legally binding agreement, hold up to their commitments, and discuss how they implement these commitments,” he said.

articles.title: India's space startups are going global. Why is that sparking debate at home?
articles.summary: A satellite startup's US defence expansion has prompted questions over whether its international operations could influence Indian government projects. Experts tell CNA why overseas business matters to the industry and how companies can balance growth with national interests.
articles.preview: A satellite startup's US defence expansion has prompted questions over whether its international operations could influence Indian government projects. Experts tell CNA why overseas business matters to the industry and how companies can balance growth with national interests. BENGALURU: For India's ambitious space startups, going global is increasingly a business necessity, say industry experts. But a recent overseas expansion has also raised questions at home about national identity, foreign ownership and control of sensitive technology.
articles.body:
A satellite startup's US defence expansion has prompted questions over whether its international operations could influence Indian government projects. Experts tell CNA why overseas business matters to the industry and how companies can balance growth with national interests.

BENGALURU: For India's ambitious space startups, going global is increasingly a business necessity, say industry experts. But a recent overseas expansion has also raised questions at home about national identity, foreign ownership and control of sensitive technology.

Bengaluru-based satellite startup Pixxel found itself at the centre of that debate recently after announcing its expansion into the United States defence and intelligence market.

The scrutiny followed Pixxel's Oct 29 announcement of a dedicated US subsidiary, Pixxel Federal, prompting questions on social media platform X about potential foreign access to sensitive technology and information linked to its Indian government projects.

The company leads a consortium selected by the Indian government in August 2025 to develop a 12-satellite Earth-observation network.

In early September, Pixxel announced a US$100 million funding round co-led by Singapore state-owned fund Temasek and British space investment firm Seraphim. Its other prominent international investor includes Google.

The debate intensified after fellow Indian space technology startup GalaxEye questioned the practice of establishing companies across jurisdictions to pursue international government contracts in a Nov 1 post on X, without naming Pixxel.

The following day, Pixxel founder Awais Ahmed rejected allegations of foreign control, insisting the company was “Indian-headquartered, Indian owned, Indian-managed and Indian-controlled”.

Other Indian space technology startups, including Digantara and Bellatrix Aerospace, have also established US subsidiaries to tap the American market and serve customers there.

Anil Prakash, director general of space body Satcom Industry Association-India (SIA-India), acknowledged that overseas expansion raised legitimate concerns over ownership, intellectual property, technology transfers and sensitive data, but said these should be assessed on “a case-by-case basis”.

“National security and international commercial expansion are not opposing objectives,” he told CNA, stressing the importance of international partnerships in building globally competitive Indian space companies.

WHY INDIAN SPACE STARTUPS ARE LOOKING OVERSEAS

For Indian rocket maker Agnikul Cosmos, global expansion is central to its business model.

The company's co-founder and COO Moin SPM said the rocket launch business depended on customers worldwide, with international demand helping companies achieve the scale and cost efficiencies needed to sustain operations.

In June, Agnikul announced a memorandum of understanding with Finnish satellite-imaging company ICEYE to explore manufacturing radar satellites in India and launching them aboard its rockets. The proposed system could support disaster monitoring and security applications, according to Moin.

But beyond accessing larger markets, Indian space startups also face financial pressures at home.

Abhishek Raju, former co-founder of satellite-data analytics company SatSure, said Indian government contracts could strain startups' cash flow despite offering valuable business opportunities.

Startups often have to provide bank guarantees and finance infrastructure and operations before receiving payments tied to project milestones, he said.

Payments can also take time to arrive even after invoices are raised, he added.

“Having an order book does not mean the companies have better cash flows. They probably have a strain on their cash flow,” Raju told CNA.

Without sufficient working capital or project financing, startups may have to raise additional venture capital, diluting their ownership, or avoid contracts with difficult payment terms.

Overseas commercial customers, Raju said, could help diversify revenue streams while giving startups access to more established financing ecosystems.

Other startups are also looking abroad for growth.

Red Balloon Aerospace, which develops high-altitude platforms for communications and surveillance, said it is working with partners in South Africa, Sweden, Spain and the United Kingdom.

Its co-founder and chief operating officer, Sireesh Pallikonda, said international markets offered greater scale and more diverse revenue streams, particularly as domestic demand could take time to translate into paying contracts.

"India offers significant long-term demand for space and defence technologies. However, sustaining growth also depends on how quickly that demand translates into commercial orders," he said.

That said, expanding overseas does not necessarily reflect a lack of domestic demand, said Prithvi Ramadhyani, a director at investment banking firm IndigoEdge.

He argued that India's defence market was already large enough to support substantial spacetech businesses, while international markets offered even greater opportunities.

Indian companies also had the technical expertise, manufacturing capabilities and cost advantages to compete globally, he added.

THE NATIONAL SECURITY BALANCING ACT

Raju said SatSure was originally headquartered in Switzerland, with an Indian subsidiary that undertook government projects.

Despite its foreign corporate structure, he said the company faced no difficulties securing contracts from Indian government organisations.

He added that India already had stringent safeguards to scrutinise companies with foreign ownership or control, particularly those involved in sensitive government projects.

“India has much stricter regulations about these things than the US or Europe.”

Raju said Indian authorities could also scrutinise companies' investors and funding sources, particularly for links to countries considered security risks.

Under India's space regulations, the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) regulates private space activities, including national-security considerations.

Foreign investors can own up to 74 per cent of Indian satellite businesses and 49 per cent of the country’s rocket manufacturers without prior government approval, while exports of sensitive technologies are regulated separately.

But Prakash of SIA-India said the growing international presence of Indian space firms required “greater clarity and predictability” in rules governing overseas subsidiaries, foreign ownership, cross-border technology transfers and companies serving government customers in multiple countries.

Balancing international expansion with national-security safeguards is not a challenge unique to India.

In the US, companies seeking access to classified defence information are assessed for foreign ownership, control or influence, according to the country’s Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency.

Similarly, Israel's Defense Export Control Agency oversees the licensing of military equipment, technology and related services sold overseas.

THE HARD PART OF GOING GLOBAL

Beyond winning international customers, Indian space startups face the challenge of securing the financing and building the track record needed to deliver complex projects.

While venture capital has helped young companies develop technology, it is less suited to financing repeated manufacturing and large contracts, according to Raju.

He said Indian space startups needed better access to bank loans, project financing and insurance to expand without repeatedly giving up ownership stakes.

The funding environment has improved, but investors remain cautious about backing technologies with uncertain commercial prospects.

Funding for Indian spacetech startups surged nearly fivefold to US$200 million in 2025 from US$43 million in 2021, according to market intelligence firm Tracxn data published in July.

“The capital to finance such risks continues to be much lower than in global markets,” IndigoEdge’s Ramadhyani said, comparing India's investment landscape with that of the US.

According to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), 67 per cent of recipients of private space-sector investment in 2025 were based in the US.

Experts said domestic contracts could help startups build credibility overseas, but converting government interest into firm orders remained challenging.

Pallikonda of Red Balloon Aerospace said paid trials, faster procurement decisions and predictable contracts would help startups establish a commercial track record.

“International customers expect proven performance, reliable delivery and long-term support,” he said.

For rocket makers such as Agnikul, this means building a track record of successful launches, which requires patient financing, consistent technical standards and access to testing infrastructure, Moin said.

As Indian space startups expand into international markets, Prakash said the challenge was to ensure a balance.

“Regulation should protect India's strategic interests without creating unnecessary barriers to innovation, investment and legitimate international business,” he said.

articles.title: Commentary: A weak South China Sea code of conduct will be worse than no agreement at all
articles.summary: As Singapore takes over as ASEAN chair in 2027, what remains unresolved on the South China Sea code of conduct are arguably the most intractable issues, says Collin Koh from the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies.
articles.preview: As Singapore takes over as ASEAN chair in 2027, what remains unresolved on the South China Sea code of conduct are arguably the most intractable issues, says Collin Koh from the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies. SINGAPORE: As the dust settles at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila with a slew of agreements, the much-anticipated Code of Conduct in the South China Sea isn’t one of them. ASEAN and China have provisionally agreed on 80 per cent of the text.
articles.body:
As Singapore takes over as ASEAN chair in 2027, what remains unresolved on the South China Sea code of conduct are arguably the most intractable issues, says Collin Koh from the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies.

SINGAPORE: As the dust settles at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila with a slew of agreements, the much-anticipated Code of Conduct in the South China Sea isn’t one of them.

ASEAN and China have provisionally agreed on 80 per cent of the text. That sounds tantalisingly close to the finishing line but the remaining 20 per cent may prove far harder to resolve.

To Manila’s credit, as the 2026 ASEAN chair, it had made finalising the code this year a key priority and oversaw intensified negotiations. China and several ASEAN members have overlapping claims in the South China Sea and maritime clashes, notably between China and the Philippines, have raised fears of escalation.

Now the hot potato is passed over to Singapore as ASEAN chair for 2027.

Secretary-General Kao Kim Hoorn said ASEAN expects talks to conclude next year. Philippine Foreign Minister Ma Theresa Lazaro also said: “I trust that Singapore will be able to finish the discussions.”

Whether this can all be finalised within next year is a huge question mark. But the pressure to finish negotiations must not come at the expense of producing a code that meaningfully reduces tensions in the South China Sea.

LAST-MILE JOURNEY MAY BE THE HARDEST

The remaining 20 per cent left unresolved represents arguably the most intractable issues.

The original single draft text adopted in 2018 was essentially a collection of the various negotiating parties’ proposals. Many concern practical security cooperation measures, such as joint efforts to deal with common threats such as aeronautical emergencies and environmental problems. Paragraphs overlapped, proposals were repeated and items continued to be subtracted or added in the years since.

It would not be presumptuous to believe that much of the progress in the past year involved the consolidation of repetitive items and tidying up this “living document”. Among the contentious issues highlighted by the Philippines in the lead-up to the summit were where the code would apply geographically and how to define the core principle of self-restraint.

On self-restraint, the code needs to clearly define what is unacceptable behaviour in the South China Sea. But the more prescriptive the “dos and don’ts”, the harder it can become to secure agreement when negotiating parties prefer flexibility to interpret such terms of references and assert national interests.

Self-restraint for Beijing, for example, is about refraining from conducting military exercises with extra-regional actors unless “parties concerned are notified beforehand and express no objection”.

ASEAN members would likely push back against a provision that could give China a de facto veto over their sovereign prerogative to pursue military cooperation with external partners. Several ASEAN countries regularly conduct maritime exercises in the South China Sea with countries like the United States, India and Japan, such as the frequent maritime cooperative activities conducted bilaterally or multilaterally between the Philippines and its foreign partners, often close to Chinese-claimed features.

These disagreements have persisted for decades. In 2002, ASEAN and China signed the Declaration of Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC) intended as a precursor to the code currently under negotiation.

Rising tensions since then make finalising the code more urgent, but at the same time, erodes the trust needed for negotiations. Leaving the notion of self-restraint open-ended would make the code no different from its 2002 precursor, and risk varying interpretations and hence potential breaches.

INEFFECTIVE WITHOUT CREDIBLE ENFORCEMENT

The code will only be effective if countries can be held to it. Whether the document would be legally-binding on all signatories remains a contentious issue.

But the question of legal status becomes almost moot, unless the parties can agree to credible measures that ensure compliance, verification and enforcement of the code. They must also agree on the appropriate institution to oversee implementation of the code and how alleged violations should be addressed.

In the original 2018 draft text, two main proposals were made - to use existing ASEAN-China meetings and working groups related to the implementation of the DOC; or to establish a dedicated commission. In either case, consensus would be required in the event of arbitrating a violation.

WHAT ASEAN RISKS WITH A WEAK AGREEMENT

So it bears asking whether all these outstanding issues can be satisfactorily addressed within one more year.

While not a formal deadline, this inevitably creates public pressures that could pull negotiations in 2027. This could come at the expense of producing a truly effective code, if the overriding objective becomes one of churning out a document to meet a perceived deadline.

A weak code would undermine peace and stability in the South China Sea. Importantly, it could undermine ASEAN’s credibility more than another delay.

This code would be a test of ASEAN’s ability to address thorny security challenges, after being often derided as nothing more than a “talk shop”. A weak code that reeks more of symbolism than substance would validate such criticism.

Collin Koh is senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, based at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore.

articles.title: Sánchez defiende en ‘Salvados’ que serán los españoles y no la “opinión publicada” quien le vuelva a hacer presidente
articles.summary: “No suelo autoengañarme y los datos tienen muy buena pinta, yo lo dejo ahí”, afirma el presidente, que se considera ganador del cara a cara con Feijóo
articles.preview: “No suelo autoengañarme y los datos tienen muy buena pinta, yo lo dejo ahí”, afirma el presidente, que se considera ganador del cara a cara con Feijóo El accidente ferroviario de Urda (Toledo) obligó a suspender la grabación, prevista el día siguiente, del regreso de Pedro Sánchez a Salvados 10 años después de la entrevista que concedió a Jordi Évole tras su dimisión como secretario general del PSOE. Sánchez se veía entonces fuera de la política tras negarse a facilitar la investidura de Mariano Rajoy.
articles.body:
“No suelo autoengañarme y los datos tienen muy buena pinta, yo lo dejo ahí”, afirma el presidente, que se considera ganador del cara a cara con Feijóo

El accidente ferroviario de Urda (Toledo) obligó a suspender la grabación, prevista el día siguiente, del regreso de Pedro Sánchez a Salvados 10 años después de la entrevista que concedió a Jordi Évole tras su dimisión como secretario general del PSOE. Sánchez se veía entonces fuera de la política tras negarse a facilitar la investidura de Mariano Rajoy. La imagen que el presidente del Gobierno ha transmitido en el programa, en el que Gonzo ha anunciado que era su última temporada, no podía ser más diferente. “No suelo autoengañarme, y los datos tienen muy buena pinta, yo lo dejo ahí. Me he presentado seis veces a las elecciones generales y no he visto esta movilización jamás”, sentencia tras poco más de una hora de conversación en la que el cara a cara con Alberto Núñez Feijóo, que se celebró la noche antes de la grabación, ha acaparado casi la mitad del tiempo.

Sánchez ha defendido sin dar ninguna muestra de dudas y nerviosismo su contención en el debate, que disparó la euforia en el PP y dejó una sensación de oportunidad perdida dentro del PSOE. El candidato socialista esgrime que su objetivo era dirigirse al electorado moderado indeciso, y que según los datos que manejan en La Moncloa y Ferraz el 29-N puede hacer ganar, o perder, no solo las elecciones sino el Gobierno. “En muchas ocasiones se piensan que un debate es como un combate de boxeo y no es así. Nada tiene que ver con eso. No es una conversación entre dos personas, al menos como yo lo interpreto es una conversación con la gente, con la ciudadanía (...) Una cosa es la opinión publicada y otra la opinión pública. Y yo creo que en la opinión pública gané el debate. Claramente de largo”, sostiene en la misma cafetería donde hace una década creyó que se despedía para siempre de las Cortes Generales. “Pero me encontré con una movilización, con una empatía, con una conexión con los afiliados de base que se convirtió en una ola de cambio que me llevó a la secretaría general del PSOE”, recuerda. Aquel ambiente de las primarias de 2017 contra Susana Díaz es lo más parecido que se percibe en los mítines socialistas, pese a los augurios funestos para sus intereses de la mayoría de casas de encuestas.

“Mi estrategia fue hablarles a aquellos que están meditando qué hacer con su voto, ya veremos el 29-N si es la acertada o no”, ha insistido Sánchez, que piensa que, “por contraste”, se vio al líder del PP como alguien “maleducado, irrespetuoso, faltón” y que “hizo de la mentira su método de debate”. “Para mí la contención significa respeto, no entrar al barro. En términos futbolísticos, no jugar como Argentina la final de la Copa del Mundo, sino jugar con juego limpio”, ha puesto como ejemplo, antes de recalcar que su “querencia” al pueblo argentino, que no es la misma" que siente por su presidente Javier Milei.

“La opinión publicada y la opinión pública no tienen por qué coincidir”, ha abundado cuando Gonzo le ha recordado algunas de las portadas de los principales medios. Sobre la de este diario, en la que un grupo de analistas daba por vencedor del cara a cara a Feijóo, ha expresado su “respeto” aunque no coincida. “A diferencia de EL PAÍS y de La Vanguardia, tanto El Mundo como La Razón me los tomo más como un tebeo”, ha dicho. Tras ser repreguntado, Sánchez ha hecho la siguiente distinción: “A los periodistas de estos dos periódicos les tengo un enorme respeto, pero la línea editorial y los titulares estaban escritos pasara lo que pasara desde la noche antes”.

La entrevista a Carles Puigdemont en el medio de Unidad Editorial el pasado jueves, en la que el expresident catalán y máximo responsable de Junts sostiene que se aprovechó de su “ambición desmedida” para imponer la ley de amnistía a cambio del apoyo de su partido a la investidura, ha sido otro de los puntos álgidos del programa. “Me pareció un poco exótica, además en El Mundo... Me parece un poco raro”, se llega a reír. “La derecha pues evidentemente en sus medios de comunicación pedaleó sobre el asunto pero no deja de ser curioso que al final den credibilidad a quien se la han negado cuando les ha interesado. ¿Cuando Puigdemont dice algo en contra de Sánchez es palabra de Dios?“, ha observado.

Sobre los motivos de la medida de gracia, el presidente ha esgrimido que la amnistía no la hizo por Puigdemont sino como “culminación de un proceso de normalización de la convivencia que le ha sentado muy bien a Cataluña”. Cuando Gonzo le ha recordado su justificación en un comité electoral del PSOE, Sánchez ha añadido que hizo “de la necesidad virtud”. “Había no solo representantes de Junts, sino funcionarios que se vieron atrapados que o se les hacía la amnistía o no iban a ver solventados sus problemas. Y había representantes de Junts que no aceptaban el indulto. Por tanto, hicimos de la necesidad virtud, porque nos permitió contar con un gobierno progresista cuatro años más”, ha argumentado.

Sánchez ha sido tajante cuando le han preguntado si aceptaría la condición de Puigdemont de celebrar un referéndum de autodeterminación en el supuesto de que volviese a depender de los votos de Junts. “No entra dentro del marco constitucional y es todo lo contrario a lo que hemos venido haciendo todo este tiempo, que es normalizar la convivencia y por tanto no dividir a la sociedad. Hoy el debate en Cataluña es sustancialmente diferente”, ha zanjado. De paso ha subrayado que en sus ocho años como presidente “se ha respetado la Constitución”. “Cuando gobernó el PP sí hubo referéndums de autodeterminación, no sabían ni donde estaban las urnas”, ha incidido sobre el desafío ilegal secesionista.

El secretario general del PSOE tampoco considera un error no haber gobernado sin aprobar unos Presupuestos, algo inédito desde la restauración de la democracia. Los vigentes son los que se aprobaron para 2023, es decir que son de la legislatura pasada. “Evidentemente es una de las prioridades de mi nueva Administración”, ha aseverado tras explicar que en esta legislatura no eran necesarios por el bazooka económico de los fondos europeos, que terminan el 31 de diciembre.

En cuanto a Óscar Puente, Sánchez le ha destacado como un “muy buen ministro de Transportes en situaciones críticas”. El dirigente socialista renunció como ministro de Transportes por el accidente de Urda, el segundo de la alta velocidad española en nueve meses tras el de Adamuz (Córdoba) con 46 víctimas mortales. “Yo que tenía mis dudas sobre la dimisión. Él tomó la decisión motu proprio, creo que hizo lo correcto al hacerlo después de aprobar las ayudas a las familiares de las víctimas, rendir cuentas en las Cortes, plantear soluciones a la quiebra de confianza en la alta velocidad y asumir las responsabilidades políticas”, ha apuntado.

A Fernando Grande Marlaska le ha defendido “junto a Alfredo Pérez Rubalcaba como los dos mejores ministros de Interior de la democracia, a años luz del ministro del Interior de la Kitchen ―la trama parapolicial de la mal denominada como policía patriótica para arrebatarle al extesorero del PP Luis Bárcenas información del partido― Jorge Fernández Díaz, que por cierto escribe en La Razón dando lecciones de ética y regeneración democrática”, ha añadido sobre otro ministro muy cuestionado.

La entrevista también ha abordado uno de los temas que más está agitando la campaña electoral: la vivienda. Sobre ello, Sánchez ha asegurado que pensó que el decreto Maricarmen iba a salir adelante. El presidente, en la conversación con Gonzo, ha explicado que posee dos pisos y los tiene alquilados, según consta en su declaración de bienes.

La parte final del programa se ha centrado en las figuras de Begoña Gómez, Santos Cerdán o José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero. Sobre su esposa, a la espera de la fecha de juicio con jurado popular tras la polémica causa dirigida por el juez ya jubilado Juan Carlos Peinado, Sánchez ha defendido su inocencia y ha lamentado lo que considera “una tremenda injusticia” por ser su pareja. “Pero si es que no hay causa. En una democracia condenar a personas inocente es lo más grave que puede suceder”, ha concluido. En una situación similar estaría su hermano, condenado a nueve años de inhabilitación por un delito de prevaricación administrativa por su contratación en 2017 en la Diputación de Badajoz.

―¿Confía en la justicia?

―No me queda más remedio que confiar en la justicia.

El escándalo protagonizado por Cerdán, el relevo de José Luis Ábalos en el área de Organización, dos personas de su total confianza que pusieron contra las cuerdas al Gobierno, le dejó “muy tocado”. “He pedido perdón por confiar en personas en quienes no debía. Es verdad que no ha sido juzgado y condenado, y hay que respetar su presunción de inocencia, pero para mí fue un momento muy duro. Sí pensé seriamente en irme y convocar elecciones. No pensé jamás que pudiera vivir una situación como esa”, asiente.

Para Zapatero solo ha tenido buenas palabras. Sánchez incluso ha compartido que habla con el expresidente, imputado en la causa del rescate de la aerolínea Plus Ultra, “regularmente sobre la campaña electoral”. “Para mí José Luis es un activo, yo defiendo su inocencia.
