articles.body:
A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in the early hours of Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel.

The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies, according to Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government.

Initial reports said several Ukrainian sea drones were launched at the ship. At least four drones were intercepted and destroyed, while two hit the warship, triggering the explosion, the officials told the Associated Press.

Satellite imagery showed the Merkury had sunk after the attack, which took place in the Mediterranean, more than 1,000 miles from south Ukraine, marking a notable geographic expansion of the now near five-year war.

Though Ukraine began the war with no navy, it has developed a sea drone capability that threatened Russian warships in the Black Sea. The Russian fleet has been forced to retreat to the eastern port of Novorossiysk because Sevastopol in occupied Crimea had become unsafe.

Hours later, a Russia-linked cargo ship said to be carrying military supplies, the Ascalon, was hit by a sea drone off the coast of Benghazi. Video showed the drone heading directly towards one end of the vessel, again causing a huge explosion.

Libyan naval forces rescued the vessel’s crew, the sources added. The health ministry said some crew members were in stable condition with minor injuries. The number of injured and their nationalities are not known.

Benghazi is controlled by the self-styled Libyan National Army, led by Gen Khalifa Haftar, which controls eastern and southern Libya and has been aligned with Russia.

There was no immediate reaction from Russian authorities, and no immediate claim of responsibility for the strike, but it comes as Ukrainian forces have stepped up their long-range attacks against Russia far beyond the frontlines.

The eastern-based Libyan authority said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe and that normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured.

It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya’s sovereignty and a threat to maritime safety, saying it would take legal and diplomatic measures against anyone found responsible.

“The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.

The specialist website Naval News earlier identified the ship attacked as the Merkury, a Russian corvette – the smallest class of warship, smaller than a frigate – and said it had almost certainly been destroyed.

HI Sutton, a naval analyst, said the attack was probably conducted by sea drones, after a photograph of one emerged apparently taken off the Libyan coast. The drone, he said, “is also likely the type used in the subsequent attack”. Similar-looking drones were involved in the subsequent attack on the Ascalon cargo ship.

If it is confirmed that Ukraine has been able to blow up or seriously damage a Russian warship in Benghazi, it would represent one of its most successful naval strikes during the almost five-year war.

But it also represents a risky extension of the fighting far beyond eastern Europe, in an incident that could affect civilians on another continent and the working of the port.

A small unit of Ukrainian special forces operatives has been based at Misrata, western Libya, and is believed to have coordinated drone attacks on Russian tankers and transport ships in the past year.

Russian ships regularly make use of the port, which has a growing military importance to the Kremlin, to supply Russian mercenary forces in Africa and as a base in the Mediterranean since the country lost its bases in Syria.

Separately, a fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was struck by drones in the Baltic Sea continued to smoulder on Sunday, Finland’s border guard said, with emergency services from Finland, Russia and Estonia working together to put out the blaze.

The Finnish military said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday was probably carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remained at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated on to a nearby Russian ship. One crew member was slightly injured.

On Sunday, visible flames had been put out, with operations focusing on cooling down the containers and stabilising the vessel, Finnish authorities said.

The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, had been damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, Finland’s defence forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials. Kyiv has sent waves of military drones towards the Leningrad region on Russia’s north-west coast this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling on to Nato territory.

The risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, could not be ruled out, Ivo Värk, the Estonian navy commander, told the public broadcaster ERR on Sunday.

Finland’s military said last week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.

articles.body:
Jay Clayton, the US director of national intelligence, said he trusts Donald Trump “completely” after the US president called Vladimir Putin “a friend” during their recent meeting in China.

Clayton made the remarks on Sunday, where he was pressed during media appearances on Trump’s warm characterization of the Russian president – who is viewed as a chief US adversary – following his trilateral summit with Putin and China’s Xi Jinping. After a backlash at home and aboard, Trump doubled down on Saturday and posted a photo of himself and Putin shaking hands with the caption “My Friend.”

On CNN’s State of the Union, Dana Bash asked Clayton whether he also thinks Putin is a friend to the US.

“The president is the greatest conductor of foreign policy in a very challenging time that we have seen,” said Clayton on Sunday. “Getting the three nuclear powers together and getting them to agree that they are not going to escalate, that they are going to communicate, that is historic. That is remarkable and, in that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely.”

Bash pressed on whether Clayton personally agrees that Putin should be considered a friend.

“Dana, in different contexts, you can use different words. The president pulling off that summit, getting the three of them together, is just remarkable,” Clayton replied.

Speaking with ABC’s Jonathan Karl on This Week, Clayton made similar comments, saying that “using the term ‘friend’ is entirely appropriate” in the context of the summit.

“That conversation, that picture – historic, historic picture – was in the context of the three nuclear powers, the three main nuclear powers, getting together and saying, ‘We cannot have a nuclear incident,’” Clayton said on Sunday, referring to Trump’s post. “In that circle of that conversation, using the term ‘friend’ is entirely appropriate.”

Clayton also dodged when asked again whether he thinks Putin should be considered a friend to the United States.

“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? He is not America’s friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all,” Clayton responded.

Last week, Trump sidestepped questions about his views on a friendship with Putin.

“I can’t speak to America,” Trump said in a press briefing. “I have fantastic relationships with Putin, that’s a very good thing.”

Trump’s characterization of Putin has sparked backlash from US lawmakers and officials abroad.

“Who is he? He’s the man who has abducted tens of thousands of children, killed tens of thousands of civilians, targeted civilian infrastructure across Ukraine, detained Americans wrongfully, and continues to do so daily,” Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer posted on social media.

“Embarrassing, despicable, and quite frankly pathetic,” Schumer added. “Senate Democrats will always stand with Ukraine and against Putin and autocratic dictators around the world.”

“It’s beyond me,” Senator Jeanne Shaheen said in an interview with MS NOW. “I don’t understand the president’s admiration and cozying up to Vladimir Putin, who is a war criminal.”

Trump’s comments also drew rebukes abroad, including from the deputy leader of the rightwing party Reform UK.

“It’s just wrong at every level … And it’s a grave mistake,” Richard Tice told Sky News. “He is not our friend, Putin. He is, as others have said, a murderous dictator. And no one is in any doubt about that.”

Trump’s description of Putin as a friend also drew criticism from European allies of Ukraine. “Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be,” the Polish prime minister Donald Tusk said.

Separately, Clayton also faced questions about the recent spate of technology outages across the US and said Americans should expect more disruptions as companies and government agencies replace aging systems.

“And as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service,” Clayton said on CNN’s State of the Union program. “That is going to happen.”

- Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
articles.summary: Libya's eastern government says the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia.
articles.preview: An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said. The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libya state media reported, citing the eastern government. The statement said there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.
articles.body:
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.

The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libya state media reported, citing the eastern government.

The statement said there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.

Later on Sunday, the health ministry said it had received injured people from another vessel, a commercial ship, that was also targeted off the coast of Benghazi, state media reported. Their injuries were minor and their condition stable, the ministry said.

Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.

US-based intelligence firm Vantor collected high-resolution images that it said showed Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette (Merkury) - a Russian navy ship - moored in the port on Saturday, and on Sunday showed most of the same ship capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible.

The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.

Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.

GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.

Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.

GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".

Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.

Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.

Although it has not been officially confirmed who was behind the attack, there is little doubt, according to Jalel Harchaoui, Libya specialist at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).

"Ukraine is the only actor brazen enough to pull something like that off," he told the BBC. "If I were to bet my own money, I would bet that it was the Ukrainians."

If confirmed, it would not be the first time Ukrainian forces had carried out an operation of this sort. In March, Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the Russian tanker Arctic Metagaz in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta with "uncrewed sea drones" launched from the Libyan coast.

As well as having an economic impact on Russia, hampering the ability of their so-called shadow fleet of tankers to export oil and gas, attacks like this are seen as humiliating to the Kremlin, according to Harchaoui.

But it is not only Moscow that will want to react to this latest incident. The ship was in the region as part of a deal with the government of eastern Libya - allied with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army.

Harchaoui said Haftar will take the attack as a personal slight. "You're going to have a response by the Haftar family. They will ask questions about who is hosting the Ukrainians."

articles.title: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
articles.summary: Finnish defence forces say that Ukraine was likely behind the drone strike on Saturday. Kyiv has yet to comment.
articles.preview: A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said. The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard. It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
articles.body:
A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.

The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.

It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.

Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.

The Sparta II was "slightly listing", Finnish authorities added, but the "situation is stable" and no fuel or other "hazardous substance leaks" had been detected.

Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.

The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.

The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.

This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.

"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."

Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

While Besprozvannykh initially said the crew of the Sparta II intended to repair the ship and carry on their journey, the Finnish Border Guard later said they had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was en route to Russia.

Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of maritime operations at the Finnish Border Guard, said during a news conference on Sunday that one Sparta II crew member had suffered minor injuries.

The Russian rescue vessel Murman is leading towing operations with the support of a Finnish guard ship and a Estonian naval patrol vessel.

Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.

Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Border Guard was responsible for the investigation into the attack and was co-operating with other relevant authorities.

Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.

The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.

Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

articles.summary: Two supertankers hit mines near Hormuz, Iranian navy says Iran's navy said on Sunday that two supertankers hit naval mines and caught fire after entering a "restricted area" east of the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian media reported. articles.title: Japan to expand kōsen education into agriculture
articles.summary: The government is also considering adding fields related to content creation, such as manga and anime, in response to demand.
articles.preview: Japan’s education ministry has compiled measures to strengthen the functions of kōsen technical colleges, featuring plans to expand their educational scope to agriculture and increase financial support for new kōsen colleges. With advances in artificial intelligence and other technologies expected to lead to a future shortage of professionals in science, engineering and digital fields, the ministry aims to encourage the establishment of more kōsen colleges to train engineers.
articles.body:
Japan’s education ministry has compiled measures to strengthen the functions of kōsen technical colleges, featuring plans to expand their educational scope to agriculture and increase financial support for new kōsen colleges.

With advances in artificial intelligence and other technologies expected to lead to a future shortage of professionals in science, engineering and digital fields, the ministry aims to encourage the establishment of more kōsen colleges to train engineers.

Kōsen are five-year higher educational institutions that students can enter after graduating from junior high school. According to the ministry, there are a total of 58 national, public and private technical colleges across Japan.

The current standards for establishing kōsen colleges, which stipulate requirements such as the number of teachers and the size of school grounds, contain no provisions for departments outside the industrial field.

To expand the scope of kōsen education, the ministry plans to introduce similar provisions for agricultural departments. It is also considering adding fields related to content creation, such as manga and anime, in response to demand.

The ministry will expand financial support for local governments and other entities seeking to establish new kōsen colleges. It plans to raise the maximum amount of subsidies to ¥4 billion from the current ¥2 billion. Nagano, Aichi and Shiga prefectures are among those taking steps to establish new kōsen colleges.

Regarding the academic title of “associate,” awarded to kōsen college graduates, the ministry is considering treating it as an internationally recognized degree.

articles.body:
Quando ascoltiamo la techno, difficilmente pensiamo a chi ha inventato quel linguaggio, agli esseri umani che ci sono dietro. Il suono delle macchine, il ronzio di fondo del sistema, quella vertigine postumana, che trasforma anche noi che balliamo in macchine senzienti, ci trascina lontano. La morte di Juan Atkins, avvenuta il 31 ottobre a Città del Messico, ci ricorda invece quanto questa musica, questo suono e quest’estetica si debbano a una persona precisa: un giovane musicista afroamericano cresciuto a Detroit che, tra la fine degli anni settanta e l’inizio degli ottanta, cominciò a immaginarsi un nuovo suono. Il soprannome The originator, l’inventore, gli è rimasto addosso per tutta la vita.

La Detroit di quegli anni era la tomba del sogno industriale, della modernità com’era stata costruita nel novecento: una città di rovine, di povertà vecchie e nuove e di quartieri segregati. E Juan Atkins non lavorava in una bolla: viveva in uno di quei quartieri e alla radio ascoltava un dj noto con il nome di The Electrifying Mojo, che accostava Parliament-Funkadelic e Kraftwerk, rendendo porosi dei confini che solo l’industria discografica considerava invalicabili.

Quel programma radiofonico era stato fondamentale anche per un altro artista del Midwest: un tale Prince Rogers Nelson, di Minneapolis. Più tardi Atkins, insieme a Derrick May e Kevin Saunderson, avrebbe dato forma alla techno di Detroit: una delle tante invenzioni afroamericane destinate a cambiare il modo di ballare del mondo. E a essere cannibalizzate da un’industria bianca.

Il successo internazionale della house di Chicago e della techno di Detroit ha spesso messo in ombra le condizioni molto locali in cui quella musica era nata. Nel suo saggio Assembling a black counter culture (Primary Information 2022), DeForrest Brown Jr. ricostruisce il conflitto tra l’autonomia dei giovani produttori di Detroit e i circuiti discografici statunitensi ed europei.

I secondi furono molto più rapidi dei primi a capire le potenzialità commerciali di quel genere di musica. Brown descrive il progetto di Underground Resistance, il collettivo della generazione successiva, come “un’impresa produttiva autogestita”: fabbricare e distribuire i propri dischi, dare voce agli abitanti neri della città e riportare opportunità nella comunità.

Il futuro tecnologico aveva bisogno anche d’infrastrutture, soldi e controllo sui mezzi per realizzarlo: Juan Atkins e gli altri lo capirono subito. Alla fine è la vecchia idea marxista del controllo dei mezzi di produzione. E di distribuzione.

E ai mezzi di produzione è ispirato il nome del progetto più famoso di Juan Atkins: Model 500, un nome che è un po’ uno pseudonimo dietro cui nascondersi e un po’ un marchio di fabbrica. Con quel nome, nel 1995, Atkins avrebbe firmato il suo album più ambizioso e sfaccettato: Deep space. Non una raccolta di singoli, come spesso avveniva nella musica dance, ma un vero album con una sua sequenza, un suo andamento e una sua estetica.

Model 500, The flow, 1995

La politica e la poetica di Atkins passavano soprattutto dall’immaginazione. In Più brillante del sole, pubblicato originariamente nel 1998 e tradotto da Alessandro Mazzi per Nero, lo scrittore britannico di origini ghanesi Kodwo Eshun scrive: “Il nome Model 500 annuncia il produttore come modello prossimo venturo, il sintetizzatore del futuro”.

Quel nome da apparecchio elettronico consentiva d’inventarsi un’identità, di sottrarsi alle aspettative su ciò che un musicista nero dovesse rappresentare. Per Eshun, “technificare significa sintetizzare la musica dagli stessi ritmi robotici che hanno messo fuori uso gli umani di Detroit”.

Le macchine che avevano trasformato il lavoro industriale fino a divorarlo diventavano strumenti per progettare un’altra esistenza. Era questo capovolgimento della macchina, da strumento di oppressione a motore per viaggiare verso un nuovo futuro, a improntare il lavoro di Juan Atkins. Viaggiare, o forse migrare.

La musica di Deep space ci ricorda anche oggi, a più di trent’anni di distanza e nel dibattito sulle intelligenze artificiali, che le macchine possiamo riprendercele, sabotarle, farle nostre: strapparle di mano a chi vorrebbe farne l’ennesimo strumento di sorveglianza e di sfruttamento.

Dipingere però la techno di Detroit solo come un’utopia libertaria e rivoluzionaria sarebbe un po’ riduttivo. Nel suo saggio “Dance dance revolution?”, pubblicato su The Baffler, lo scrittore e regista Hubert Adjei-Kontoh ci fa riflettere sulle fratture di classe interne alla prima scena di Detroit, frequentata anche da ragazzi della borghesia nera che volevano tenere lontani dai loro party i coetanei poveri.

Erano state le conquiste sindacali dell’industria automobilistica della città a creare il benessere necessario per sperimentare. Se un ragazzo nero di Detroit poteva comprarsi un sintetizzatore Korg MS-10, molto spesso alle spalle aveva una famiglia di operai specializzati che avevano raggiunto un certo livello, per quanto fragile, di benessere. È un paradosso da tenere presente: riconoscere la storia nera della techno di Detroit significa anche prendere sul serio le sue contraddizioni.

In Europa la techno trovò un mercato più ricettivo. Deep space, infatti, uscì per la R&S, un’etichetta belga nata a Gand nel 1983 su iniziativa di Renaat Vandepapeliere e Sabine Maes. Vandepapeliere chiamò i numeri di telefono stampati sulle etichette di quei dischi pazzeschi e futuristici che arrivavano da Detroit. In questo modo entrò in contatto con i padri fondatori della techno: Juan Atkins, Derrick May e Kevin Saunderson. Quegli scambi contribuirono a creare un ponte culturale tra Detroit e l’Europa.

Una musica mai sentita prima

La ricchezza di suoni e la dinamica di Deep space sono sconvolgenti: ascoltarlo nel 1995 significava avvicinarsi a una musica mai sentita prima. Ancora oggi fa lo stesso effetto. La cassa regolare tiene la rotta, mentre tutto intorno si muovono bassi elastici, percussioni secche e linee di sintetizzatore che allargano l’orizzonte.

L’eredità electro degli anni ottanta sembra sublimarsi in un suono più spazioso, dove la precisione delle sequenze lascia respirare le melodie. La parola techno rischia di far pensare soltanto a qualcosa di robotico, d’industriale, di asettico e artificiale. Qui invece la macchina riesce a sognare e a immaginare se stessa come qualcosa di organico, quasi fosse uscita da un romanzo di Philip K. Dick.

Nella musica una figura torna e cambia significato, un ritmo ostinato diventa un ambiente da abitare. A fare da motore immobile di tutto è soprattutto il funk, che ci ancora alla realtà anche quando la musica sembra lanciarsi nello spazio. Model 500 non fa che proporci una versione aumentata e aggiornata della Mothership, l’astronave madre con cui, negli anni settanta, i Parliament-Funkadelic partivano per il loro viaggio afrofuturistico e liberatorio nello spazio.

Gran parte dell’album nasce dalla collaborazione con Moritz von Oswald, percussionista, compositore e figura centrale della scena berlinese. La techno di Deep space è fatta da musicisti che s’incontrano, condividono strumenti e lavorano sul suono.

Nel 2013 Atkins ricordava su Electronic Beats la meraviglia provata davanti al sistema con cui von Oswald sincronizzava vecchie apparecchiature di marche diverse. Dietro a quel viaggio cosmico c’è anche questo: trovare il modo di far dialogare e interagire tra loro delle macchine. Allora sembrava fantascienza, oggi è la nostra quotidianità.

Riascoltato dopo la morte di Atkins, Deep space conserva una strana forma di familiarità, quasi d’intimità. Il futuro che immaginava è diventato in parte il nostro paesaggio sonoro, ma l’album mantiene aperta una possibilità che oggi facciamo fatica a vedere: usare la tecnologia per fabbricarsi una vita diversa e una visione dell’universo più vasta, anziché una prigione. Un giovane musicista di Detroit si era costruito un’astronave con i suoi sintetizzatori. Trent’anni dopo possiamo ancora salirci per partire alla scoperta dello spazio profondo. ◆

articles.title: Nigerian youth have shown their power in the past - why aren't they shaping this election?
articles.summary: Fewer young people have registered to vote in next year's election than in 2023 - are young people losing faith in democracy?

articles.body:
Abdulhadi Dalhatu is something of a rarity in Nigeria politics.

At 38, he is among the young people seeking elected office in a country where about 80% of the population is under 40.

He hopes his age will stand in his favour as he campaigns for a seat in the state assembly in the northern Kano state in January's general elections.

"Younger people are the majority in this country and should be deciding the future," Dalhatu tells the BBC.

But Nigeria's political history suggests he faces an uphill battle.

Since the return to civilian rule in 1999, Goodluck Jonathan has been the youngest person elected president, taking office at the age of 53.

The current president, Bola Tinubu, is 74 and would be 79 by the end of a second term if he is re-elected in January.

His main challengers are also considerably older. Atiku Abubakar, seeking the presidency for the seventh time, is 79, while Peter Obi is 65.

Of the 18 presidential candidates, only one is under 40 - Moses Olusoji Adebisi, a 35-year-old businessman representing the Democratic Leadership Alliance (DLA).

Although he says he is confident of winning, few Nigerians appear to know much about him and he has not been seen much on the campaign trail.

The contrast is striking in a country with one of the world's youngest populations, where young people have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to shape political debate and mobilise for change.

In the previous election, Obi, then 61, galvanised millions of young Nigerians through a social media-driven movement known as the "Obedients".

His campaign promised a break from the established political order, appealing particularly to young people struggling to find jobs and earn a decent living.

But his failure to win the presidency left many of his supporters disillusioned.

"At the time we were so hopeful, but unfortunately the result wasn't what we wanted, which made many lose hope in the system," former Obedient Nonso Chukwudi tells the BBC.

The movement had built on the momentum of the EndSars protests in 2020, which grew into one of Nigeria's biggest youth-led movement in decades.

Initially sparked by anger over police brutality, the demonstrators developed into a wider call for political reform, accountability and greater youth participation in governance.

But the protests were eventually crushed by the authorities. About 56 were reportedly killed, although officials dispute this figure, while hundreds were arrested and some had their bank accounts frozen.

Both EndSars and the Obedients demonstrated the capacity of young Nigerians to mobilise around political causes.

But turning that enthusiasm into sustained electoral participation has proved much harder.

Hajara Musa, 33, is among those who have lost faith in the political system. She has no plans to register or vote in the near future.

"I just feel like things are already determined and I'll just be wasting my time. It is going to be the same people all over again," she tells the BBC.

The electoral register appears to reflect this growing disillusionment.

Although the number of registered voters has increased by 10 million to over 103 million since the last election, enrolment of those under 35 has actually fallen, by about seven million.

Young people now account for just 29% of registered voters, down from 40% in 2023.

Nigeria's electoral commission, Inec, says it has made efforts to encourage more young people to register ahead of the 2027 general elections.

This includes appointing nine ambassadors from the entertainment industry, spanning film, music and comedy, to reach younger audiences.

But the figures suggest these efforts have yet to make a significant difference.

Dalhatu says he understands the frustration but argues that young Nigerians cannot expect change, if they stay away from the political process.

"Unfortunately, many prefer to just post on social media" instead of getting involved, he says.

Of course being young does not mean you are necessarily the best candidate.

For those who want to participate, there is a formidable obstacle to getting into politics - money.

Dalhatu dreams of becoming president one day, but says he has previously had to abandon campaigns because he could not raise enough funds.

The cost of running for office in Nigeria is notoriously high.

Under the Electoral Act, presidential candidates were allowed to spend up to 5bn naira (£2.8m; $3.7m) on campaigns ahead of the 2023 elections. That spending limit has since been doubled.

The cost of nomination forms alone puts the presidency beyond the reach of most aspiring young Nigerians.

The ruling All Progressive Congress (APC), along with the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and the African Democratic Congress (ADC) have each set their presidential nomination fee at 100m naira ($74,000; £56,000), making it extremely hard for new challengers to emerge.

Since the return to democracy in 1999, only two parties have governed Nigeria - the PDP from 1999 to 2015 and the APC since 2015.

These parties, alongside the ADC, formed last year by politicians who had defected from the other two, have established nationwide network of branches, supporters and campaigners.

Those aspiring candidates without the financial resources to secure nomination forms and compete in the internal party contests of the main parties have little chances of becoming president.

The barriers are also evident in the National Assembly.

Not one of Nigeria's 109 senators is under 40, while only 14 of the 360 members of the House of Representatives fall into that age group.

"I have been in politics for many years and I will tell you that young people in this country lack the resources to become president," says Dalhatu, who is running under Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress.

Fatima Zahra Umar, a young politician in the APC who has previously tried to run for a seat in the House of Representatives, agrees.

"Young Nigerians are poor. Nigerian politics is cash-intensive, so participation is guided by money," she says, adding that young people are often content with having a bit of influence as a special advisor to a senior politician.

But political analyst Seun Ajayi believes the problems go beyond the financial barriers.

"We have some of the most brilliant young persons in the world, but they are either not interested in politics or feel satisfied when given a small role in government," he says.

"The old men are not going to sit idle and allow us to push them out. We have to fight for the big positions, but at the moment I don't see the zeal."

Umar believes changing attitudes towards young leadership is equally important.

"Culturally, we are not primed to trust or accept the brilliance of a younger person, so it will be very difficult," she says.

"Old men are still holding on to the system."

Some Nigerians took inspiration from the wave of success of young candidates in the recent midterm elections in the US, some of whom have roots in Africa.

"America Has Done It, Can Nigerians Do the Same?" entertainer Charly Boy wrote on X, in a post that was widely shared.

He said the US results served as a warning to Nigerian politicians that no matter how powerful the political machine, voters can change the direction of government.

He called on young people to interrogate candidates about their past promises: "Has life improved? Where are the jobs, security and affordable living?

"Democracy is not a spectator sport, nor is it about sharing rice," he wrote.

articles.title: Morte Gianni De Gennaro, la politica sotto choc: il cordoglio di Mattarella e Meloni
articles.summary: AGI - Servitore dello Stato, uomo delle istituzioni, figura di primo piano degli apparati di sicurezza. La politica è scossa dalla morte di Gianni De Gennaro, l'ex capo della Polizia che aveva collaborato con il giudice Giovanni Falcone ed era finito nell'inchiesta di Caltanissetta sul depistaggio delle indagini sulla strage di via D'Amelio, nella quale persero la vita il giudice Paolo Borsellino e gli agenti della sua scorta. Il corpo è stato ritrovato nella sua casa di campagna in provincia di Grosseto. I familiari non avevano sue notizie da ore e non riuscivano a raggiungerlo. Quindi l'allarme e la scoperta della morte. Secondo quanto riferito, si sarebbe trattato di un suicidio. Il cordoglio di Mattarella e Meloni Il presidente della Repubblica ha chiamato il comandante generale della Guardia di Finanza, Andrea De Gennaro, fratello di Gianni De Gennaro, per esprimere il proprio cordoglio in forma riservata. Anche la presidente del Consiglio, Giorgia Meloni, si rivolge ad Andrea De Gennaro e a tutti i familiari, dicendosi "profondamente scioccata dalla tragica scomparsa". E così il sottosegretario alla Presidenza del Consiglio, Alfredo Mantovano: "Sono sconvolto per la tragica morte di un servitore dello Stato, con il quale ho avuto modo di collaborare per anni e di cui ho ammirato le doti, il senso delle istituzioni e la dedizione al dovere". Il ministro dell'Interno, Matteo Piantedosi, ne ricorda "la serietà, la competenza e la dedizione", sottolineando come la scomparsa di "un grande funzionario dello Stato sconvolge e lascia sgomenti". La Russa e Fontana: prudenza nei giudizi e rispetto della dignità La morte di De Gennaro riapre il dibattito sulla riservatezza delle indagini e sulla prudenza nei giudizi. "Fino a quando non c'è un giudizio definitivo nessuno è condannato, credo che anche in questa tristissima vicenda ci sia modo di riflettere", dice il presidente del Senato, Ignazio La Russa. Sulla stessa linea il presidente della Camera: "Una vicenda drammatica che richiama una riflessione sulla necessaria prudenza nei giudizi e sul rispetto della dignità di ogni persona", avverte Lorenzo Fontana. Salvini e Vannacci criticano i processi mediatici Contro quelli che definiscono processi mediatici intervengono il vicepremier Matteo Salvini e il leader di Futuro Nazionale, Roberto Vannacci. "Sono sconvolto per la notizia della morte di un leale servitore dello Stato come Gianni De Gennaro, vittima di un massacro mediatico-giudiziario che una persona e una carriera come la sua non meritavano", dice Salvini. "Un servitore dello Stato vittima di quei processi mediatici giocati fuori dalle aule dei tribunali e molto cari a una certa stampa faziosa", rincara Vannacci. Per La Russa, tuttavia, occorre un supplemento di riflessione prima di trarre conclusioni sulle ragioni che hanno portato Gianni De Gennaro alla morte. A chi gli chiede se il suicidio sia dovuto a un momento di fragilità, la seconda carica dello Stato risponde con un invito alla cautela: "Prima di dire che il suicidio è fragilità ci rifletterei". Anche il ministro della Difesa, Guido Crosetto, respinge l'idea di una fragilità di fondo: "Forse il suo è stato l'ultimo coraggioso atto di servizio: non poteva accettare che qualcuno sporcasse quella storia che non era solo sua, ma delle istituzioni che ha servito". Le opposizioni: è il momento del rispetto e del silenzio Dalle opposizioni l'invito, quasi unanime, è al rispetto e al silenzio. "Oggi è il giorno del silenzio e del rispetto umano. La morte dell'ex capo della Polizia Gianni De Gennaro lascia tutti sgomenti. Il nostro cordoglio ai suoi familiari. Ci saranno tempi e modi per entrare nel merito di quanto sta accadendo", afferma Giuseppe Conte. La morte di Gianni De Gennaro è "un fatto sconvolgente, davanti a cui è il momento del rispetto del dolore dei familiari e in questo senso mandiamo loro il nostro cordoglio", sono le parole della segretaria del Pd, Elly Schlein.

articles.summary: Finland's Defense Ministry thinks the incursion is linked to a drone strike earlier Saturday on a Russian cargo ship, which is on a US sanctions list.

A Russian helicopter is suspected of violating Finnish airspace, the Nordic country's Ministry of Defense said Saturday. The incident happened a few hours after a drone attack left a Russian cargo ship ablaze in the Gulf of Finland, the easternmost part of the Baltic Sea. What do we know?
articles.body:
Finland says Russian helicopter violated its airspace

November 21, 2026

Finland's Defense Ministry thinks the incursion is linked to a drone strike earlier Saturday on a Russian cargo ship, which is on a US sanctions list.

A Russian helicopter is suspected of violating Finnish airspace, the Nordic country's Ministry of Defense said Saturday.

The incident happened a few hours after a drone attack left a Russian cargo ship ablaze in the Gulf of Finland, the easternmost part of the Baltic Sea.

What do we know?

According to Finland's Defense Ministry, the incursion happened at 12:34 p.m. local time (10:34 UTC/GMT) off the town of Loviisa, on the southern coast.

"This alleged airspace violation may be linked to rescue or surveillance operations carried out by Finland following damage sustained by a cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland," public broadcaster YLE cited Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen as saying.

The ministry added the helicopter could have penetrated up to 4.1 kilometers (2.5 miles) into Finnish territory.

What do we know about the cargo ship attack?

Earlier Saturday, Finland — one of NATO's newest members — said a Russian cargo ship heading for Russia's Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad caught fire after being struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland.

The Finnish military said the Sparta II was damaged west of Russia's Gogland island, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from Finland's coast, and later drifted into Finnish territorial waters.

Finnish Border Guard Commander Ilja Iljin later told YLE that the vessel, which is known to have links to the Russian military, was struck by Ukrainian drones while in Russian waters.

"At the moment, there is no confirmed information about what cargo is on board, but it cannot be ruled out that there is military materiel on board," Iljin said.

The ship is on a US sanctions list, according to a search of the Open Sanctions website.

The Border Guard later said the crew of the Sparta II was evacuating into a life raft and rescue boat.

Orpo backs Ukraine against 'aggressor'

"The [Ukraine] war is spilling over into our neighbouring areas," wrote Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo on X.

Ukraine has the right to fight against the aggressor," he added.

The Finnish government has put temporary curbs on aviation and maritime traffic in the eastern Gulf of Finland.

The Defense Ministry said Finland had informed its allies about the incident.

articles.title: New EU budget proposal aims at tax gobal tech giants
articles.summary: European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a smaller EU budget for 2028-2034, including a 3% tax on major digital firms to ease member states' contributions. France has already rejected the plan as inadequate.
articles.preview: EU takes aim at tech giants in tax proposal November 21, 2026 European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a smaller EU budget for 2028-2034, including a 3% tax on major digital firms to ease member states' contributions. France has already rejected the plan as inadequate. European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a new draft for the next EU budget. Among other things, he is suggesting a tax on big tech firms to ease the contributions of member states, some of which strongly criticised earlier proposals.
articles.body:
EU takes aim at tech giants in tax proposal

November 21, 2026

European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a smaller EU budget for 2028-2034, including a 3% tax on major digital firms to ease member states' contributions. France has already rejected the plan as inadequate.

European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a new draft for the next EU budget.

Among other things, he is suggesting a tax on big tech firms to ease the contributions of member states, some of which strongly criticised earlier proposals.

The EU budget is theEuropean Union’s shared budget and it is used for things ranging from agricultural subsidies, infrastructure projects to border control and defence.

A first draft for the 2028 to 2034 budget was proposed by the EU Commission in 2025 but was criticised, especially by a group of northern European members including Germany who wanted the budget to be much smaller.

Following that criticism, the European Council President has now suggested a new draft, which is smaller by €204 billion.

But divisions among member states appear to remain, with France immediately coming out against Costa’s new draft, saying it was "deeply disappointing."

What’s the plan for the tech tax?

The proposal includes a string of new "revenue channels," explicitly intended to "to keep national contributions at a reasonable level," so that member state will have to contribute less than otherwise would be the case.

The biggest splash would likely come from a tax on companies with an annual turnover from digital activities of at least 50 million euros in the EU and 750 million euros worldwide.

Those firms would be subject to "an annual contribution corresponding to 3% of the annual net turnover from online advertising, digital intermediation services and user-generated data," according to Costa.

Aside from the tech tax, the "balanced basket of new own resources" also includes taxes on tobacco products and electronic waste.

What happens next?

Neither the EU Commission nor European Council President Costa will have the final word on the budget. Costa's plan will now be at the centre of hours of talks when EU leaders meet in Brussels next week.

"This is a realistic budget that addresses our new priorities while preserving our established policies," Costa wrote about his proposal. "I am confident that this proposal is a good basis for moving towards a final agreement."

But an initial reaction from France suggests that any final agreement might still be some way off.

The French presidency said the budget "falls well short of what is needed, particularly on the Common Agricultural Policy, notably to guarantee income support for farmers."

"As it stands, this proposal from the President of the European Council does not provide a basis for an agreement."

The EU was hoping to reach a general agreement on the budget by the end of 2026 with its formal adoption planned for 2027.

articles.title: South Africa's former vice president and UN official dies aged 71
articles.summary: Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka was the country's first deputy president and headed UN Women from 2013 to 2021.
articles.preview: South Africa Tributes have been pouring in for South Africa's first female deputy president, Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, who has died at the age of 71. A statement from her family said she passed away on Friday following complications from a medical procedure she underwent about two weeks ago. She served as South Africa's deputy president from 2005 to 2008, having previously worked as minerals and energy minister.

She served as South Africa's deputy president from 2005 to 2008, having previously worked as minerals and energy minister.

The former deputy VP also had stints as United Nations under-secretary-general and headed its agency for gender equality, UN Women, from 2013 to 2021.

She has been praised for her decades-long work on social justice as well as the rights of women.

"Our hearts are really, really sad and broken for having lost such a very dynamic woman leader in our country," President Cyril Ramaphosa said.

"She truly flew the flag of women, not only women of South Africa and Africa, but women of the world," he said.

In a statement on X, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres praised Mlambo-Ngcuka as a "lifelong champion of the rights & empowerment of women and girls".

She "believed that gender equality is not a favour to be granted, but a right to be claimed", he said.

UN Women also paid tribute, lauding her courage and leadership, saying she inspired people around the world.

UN Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed recalled Mlambo-Ngcuka’s interventions on behalf of women and girls in Afghanistan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Nigeria.

"She pushed the limits and I think that that's where we got a lot of the confidence to do the things that we do, following in her footsteps," she said.

South African parliamentary officials, unions, and political parties have all been among those expressing their condolences.

articles.title: Kiev: 'Il bilancio dell'attacco russo a Dymer è salito a sei morti'
articles.summary: Nave militare russa colpita a Bengasi, 'sono stati gli ucraini'
articles.preview: Il bilancio delle vittime dell'attacco di un drone russo a un edificio di cinque piani a Dymer, nella regione di Kiev, è salito a sei. I soccorritori continuano a rimuovere le macerie. Lo riporta Rbc-Ucraina, citando il capo dell'amministrazione statale regionale di Kiev, Timur Tkachenko. articles.body:
Il bilancio delle vittime dell'attacco di un drone russo a un edificio di cinque piani a Dymer, nella regione di Kiev, è salito a sei. I soccorritori continuano a rimuovere le macerie. Lo riporta Rbc-Ucraina, citando il capo dell'amministrazione statale regionale di Kiev, Timur Tkachenko. Il Servizio statale per le emergenze ha reso noto che i soccorritori hanno estratto il corpo della sesta vittima dalle macerie di una casa distrutta.

Tkachenko ha espresso le sue condoglianze alla famiglia del defunto, precisando che le operazioni di ricerca e soccorso sono tuttora in corso. Il precedente bilancio parlava di quattro morti.

Una nave militare russa ormeggiata nella base navale Bengasi è stata colpita in un attacco con droni. L'esplosione non ha fatto vittime, ma dieci persone sono rimaste ferite e la corvetta è stata quasi distrutta. Il raid ha provocato la reazione del governo della Libia orientale guidato da Osama Hammad che parla di una " grave aggressione alla sovranità nazionale". Dietro l'attacco, per il giornalista di Axios Barak Ravid, c'è la mano del Servizio di sicurezza dell'Ucraina (Sbu) in un'escalation che per la prima volta tocca una nave militare russa nel Mediterraneo, dove in passato erano stati colpiti solo mercantili o petroliere della "flotta ombra" di Mosca.

A sole 24 ore dall'attacco alla nave russa nel golfo di Finlandia, la guerra nei mari dunque si allarga, colpendo a oltre 3.000 chilometri di distanza. Mentre i raid continuano a mietere vittime anche sul terreno: un attacco russo ha colpito un condominio a Dymer, cittadina rurale a 45 chilometri a nord di Kiev. E' l'ennesima strage: tre morti sono già stati estratti dalle macerie, e almeno 11 persone mancano all'appello. Altre tre vittime si registrano nella regione della capitale.

La nave colpita sulle coste africane era la corvetta della marina militare russa Merkury, classe Steregushchiy. Scortava cargo ed era diretta in Russia. Aveva fatto scalo a Bengasi per rifornirsi di carburante e viveri, nell'ambito degli accordi di cooperazione tra Libia e Russia. "La Libia non è parte della guerra russo-ucraina né di alcun altro conflitto armato al di fuori dei propri confini", ha affermato il governo di Bengasi che ha avviato un'inchiesta in coordinamento con le autorità russe, avvertendo che non permetterà "che i porti, il territorio o le acque territoriali della Libia siano trasformati in un'arena per regolamenti di conti o per l'esportazione di conflitti".

Sul fronte diplomatico intanto non si registrano passi in avanti nei negoziati, anche se l'amministrazione Usa continua a spingere per un accordo di pace entro gennaio, prima che il Congresso a maggioranza Dem si insedi. Zelensky aveva spiegato che gli Stati Uniti hanno proposto un incontro a livello di leader già prima di Natale. Ma una data ufficiale non è ancora stata fissata, mentre sono in corso sforzi diplomatici per tenere un incontro ai vertici a margine del vertice del G20 del 14-15 dicembre a Miami, a cui però l'Ucraina non è - per il momento - invitata.

Nel frattempo il presidente americano Donald Trump continua la sua luna di miele con il presidente russo, Vladimir Putin, tornando a definirlo in un post su Truth 'il mio amico'. Parole che hanno suscitato un'ondata di polemiche, a partire dallo stesso Zelensky. Il presidente ucraino, alla domanda se il tycoon l'abbia mai chiamato "amico", ha risposto secco: "Penso di sì... il problema è che non me lo ricordo".

Più tagliente ancora il viceministro britannico con delega per gli Affari europei, Hamish Falconer, secondo cui Putin altro non è che un "macellaio". Caustico sui commenti l'inviato presidenziale russo, Kirill Dmitriev: "Regno Unito, Unione Europea, guerrafondai, progressisti e liberali sono tutti in preda al panico per il post del presidente Trump", ma "ottimi rapporti tra Trump e il presidente Putin sono vitali per la sicurezza, la pace e la prosperità del mondo".

articles.summary: Eisenkot condemns 'Jewish terrorism' near Ramallah as US congressman calls for accountability Israeli politician Gadi Eisenkot has condemned a series of arson attacks by settlers in the occupied West Bank as "Jewish terrorism", accusing far-right ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben Gvir of fuelling violence against Palestinians. "The acts of sabotage carried out by extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes undermine regional stability, endanger lives and seriously harm Israel's national security and foreign relations," he wrote on X. Opposition leader Yair Lapid also condemned the attacks, calling them "Jewish terrorism" caused by government negligence. In the United States, Democratic Congressman Josh Gottheimer condemned the attacks and called for accountability. "These incidents warrant a full and thorough investigation," Gottheimer wrote on X, adding that vigilante justice had "no place" in society. articles.title: Iran unveils new launcher that can fire two missiles at once
articles.summary: Iran unveils new launcher that can fire two missiles at once Iran has unveiled a new missile launcher, as senior military commanders touted the Islamic Republic's capabilities in defiant messages to the United States. "A launcher capable of firing two liquid-propellant missiles simultaneously was unveiled for the first time," Iranian state television reported on Saturday. State television broadcast footage of Ahmad Vahidi, commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), and Majid Mousavi, head of the IRGC's Aerospace Force, touring an underground missile base. The two commanders were shown riding on top of a vehicle through long tunnels lined with missiles, launchers and other military equipment. "The damage suffered by our enemy is only the beginning. We shall witness their humiliation," Vahidi said. "Our capabilities have grown during the last two conflicts, and our high-performance weaponry can intimidate the enemy," said Mousavi. During the US-Israeli war on Iran, strikes targeted the country's missile capabilities and hit its nuclear sites for a second time, though the extent of the damage remains unclear. Earlier this month, the IRGC unveiled what it described as new underground "missile cities" housing ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as launchers. articles.title: A nuoto per tre giorni a Hormuz, 'basta guerra e inquinamento'
articles.summary: L'azione dimostrativa di un 56enne britannico tra 'petroliere in fiamme ed esplosioni'
articles.preview: A nuoto per tre giorni attraverso le acque di Hormuz, avanzando a bracciate lungo 15 chilometri per trasmettere un messaggio di pace forte e chiaro: "Basta combattimenti. Aprite lo Stretto. Ripulitelo dall'inquinamento". E' la missione in cui si è lanciato Lewis Pugh, 56enne britannico specializzato in nuoto di resistenza, e conclusa nella giornata di sabato, come riportato dal Guardian e altri media internazionali.
articles.body:
A nuoto per tre giorni attraverso le acque di Hormuz, avanzando a bracciate lungo 15 chilometri per trasmettere un messaggio di pace forte e chiaro: "Basta combattimenti. Aprite lo Stretto. Ripulitelo dall'inquinamento". E' la missione in cui si è lanciato Lewis Pugh, 56enne britannico specializzato in nuoto di resistenza, e conclusa nella giornata di sabato, come riportato dal Guardian e altri media internazionali.

Già protagonista di altre lunghe traversate volte a sensibilizzare su cause politiche sociali (ad esempio al Polo Nord) Pugh, che è anche riconosciuto come ambasciatore degli Oceani dalle Nazioni Unite, ha scelto per la prima volta di nuotare in una zona di conflitto. Perché, come lui stesso ha spiegato in un post su Instagram, la situazione dell'area di Hormuz è ora emblema di due delle questioni che più preoccupano il pianeta: i conflitti bellici e la crisi climatica, che in quel tratto di mare si incrociano.

"La guerra provoca immense sofferenze umane. Si perdono vite, famiglie vengono distrutte e case rase al suolo. Ma c'è un'altra vittima a cui viene dedicata fin troppo poca attenzione: la natura stessa", afferma Pugh. Questo stretto che separa le coste dell'Oman e dell'Iran è infatti "una delle grandi meraviglie del mondo", con le sue "montagne imponenti che si innalzano su fiordi spettacolari". Ma ora "questo luogo straordinario si trova nel mezzo di un conflitto", con "petroliere, navi metaniere e altre imbarcazioni commerciali che vengono attaccate". Una crisi le cui "conseguenze ambientali dureranno per decenni".

Pugh, che ha nuotato in un braccio di mare compreso tra l'isola di Musandam e Capo Hormuz, lungo il lato omanita dello Stretto, ha detto di esser stato diretto testimone di episodi che dimostrano cosa sta accadendo lì. "Appena 30 minuti dopo aver iniziato a nuotare, una petroliera è stata colpita a pochi chilometri di distanza. Le esplosioni hanno fatto tremare il mare intorno a me. Nei giorni successivi, ho assistito ad altri attacchi contro il traffico marittimo commerciale e ho visto alcune imbarcazioni avvolte dalle fiamme", ha raccontato. Ora chiede aiuto per "diffondere il messaggio" contro la guerra e contro l'inquinamento che provoca.

articles.body:
Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader, who described them as “Jewish terrorism”.

Dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday, setting fire to about a dozen vehicles and several homes and scrawling racist graffiti. At least four communities were attacked. Israeli police said they had launched an investigation with forensic teams.

Photographs from Kafr Malik, near Ramallah, showed one slogan written in Hebrew that read: “This is the first revenge.” Several vehicles and homes had been set alight in the village.

Images from nearby Deir al-Sudan showed vehicles on fire. Palestinian reports said an agricultural building had been set ablaze in Deir Ballut and cars torched in Deir Abu Mashal.

An inconclusive election last month stripped Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister, of his majority. Eisenkot has been asked to form a government, though his prospects seem little better.

“Last night’s arson attacks in Judea and Samaria were acts of Jewish terrorism, in every sense of the term,” Eisenkot said, using the biblical name for the West Bank. “Extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes are undermining regional stability, putting lives at risk and doing grave damage to Israel’s national security and foreign relations.”

Referring to the far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, he added: “The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy.”

Eisenkot, who has been given 28 days to form a government by the president, Isaac Herzog, with a possible 14-day extension, urged the government and security establishment to “use every tool at their disposal – including administrative detention and targeted operations by the Shin Bet – to stop the rioters and impose harsh sanctions on them”.

In an unprecedented rebuke on Sunday, several other members of the Israeli parliament criticised Netanyahu over escalating violence by militant settlers against Palestinians.

Yair Lapid, the leader of Yesh Atid, held Netanyahu’s government responsible for encouraging the attacks. “Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence by the Israeli government,” he said on X, adding that ministers were deliberately encouraging the militant settlers’ violence “through their silence”.

Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats party, warned of the possibility of a third intifada and described the West Bank as “on the brink of an explosion”.

“Anyone who wants to prevent a third intifada must replace the current government, which provides cover and support for Jewish terrorism and abandons security,” Golan said on X. “Jewish terrorism harms innocent Palestinians and Israeli army soldiers, and pushes Israel toward unprecedented international isolation.”

Noam Tibon, a retired army major general and Knesset member, gave a similar warning. “If Israel does not eliminate Jewish terrorism in the West Bank, it will destroy Israel,” he wrote.

Netanyahu has not yet responded to the accusations.

Australia announced sanctions on Wednesday against three people and four Israeli entities, including a construction company, over their role in the expansion of illegal settlements and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

A day earlier the UK imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building illegal settlements in the West Bank, which the UN regards as Palestinian territory under Israeli occupation since 1967.

Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.

On Tuesday, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli militant settlers in a village near Jericho, where the group has recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.

Reuters contributed to this report

articles.title: Briton swims length of strait of Hormuz to highlight environmental cost of war
articles.summary: UN patron Lewis Pugh saw ships ablaze and fighter jets overhead during three-day swim as Iran conflict continues A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the strait of Hormuz to highlight the environmental cost of the Iran war. Lewis Pugh, a UN patron of the oceans, swam the 9.3-mile (15km) length of the waterway, which is a key route for oil shipments from the Middle East. Continue reading...
articles.preview: UN patron Lewis Pugh saw ships ablaze and fighter jets overhead during three-day swim as Iran conflict continues A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the strait of Hormuz to highlight the environmental cost of the Iran war. Lewis Pugh, a UN patron of the oceans, swam the 9.3-mile (15km) length of the waterway, which is a key route for oil shipments from the Middle East. Continue reading...
articles.body:
A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the strait of Hormuz to highlight the environmental cost of the Iran war.

Lewis Pugh, a UN patron of the oceans, swam the 9.3-mile (15km) length of the waterway, which is a key route for oil shipments from the Middle East.

According to the Lewis Pugh Foundation, he witnessed several attacks on commercial shipping, explosions in the distance and fighter jets overhead.

An oil tanker was struck by a projectile about 2.5 miles from where he was swimming on the first day. On the second, he saw flames rising above a headland separating him from a burning liquefied petroleum gas carrier, Tara Gas, and later he passed close to the vessel while it was still on fire.

“My immediate thoughts were for the seafarers onboard,” Pugh said. “The flames were enormous. These vessels carry highly flammable gases, and an attack on one can have catastrophic consequences, not just for crew members but also on the surrounding marine environment.”

The 56-year-old undertook his first swim in a conflict zone to urge an end to the fighting, the reopening of the strait and action to address environmental damage caused by the conflict.

Believed to be the first person to attempt a long-distance swim in the strait since the conflict began in March, Pugh swam a route from Musandam Island, carving through the dramatic mountains and inlets of Oman’s Musandam peninsula and Iran’s spectacular mangrove forests, to reach the Cape of Hormuz at the peninsula’s northern tip.

He said: “War causes immense human suffering. Lives are lost, families are torn apart and homes, hospitals and schools can be destroyed in minutes. But there is another casualty that receives far too little attention: nature itself. And the damage can last long after the fighting has stopped.”

The small expedition team included a support boat and kayak that remained alongside Pugh during the swim.

Pugh said environmental damage caused by conflict often received less attention than the human cost. According to the UN, at least 175 vessels have been attacked since fighting began, and about 30 attacks have caused significant pollution.

The strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most important shipping routes and is also home to wildlife including dugongs, sea turtles and whale sharks.

Pugh, who was born in Plymouth, said oil spills and other contamination could have long-term consequences for marine ecosystems including coral reefs, seagrass meadows and mangrove forests.

articles.title: Ukraine: Up to seven feared trapped beneath rubble near Kyiv after Russian attack
articles.summary: A Russian strike partially destroyed an apartment building in Dymer, north of Kyiv, on Sunday. Nine people, including a child, were evacuated as rescuers searched the rubble for up to seven others feared trapped.
articles.preview: Emergency workers rushed to the scene in Dymer, near Kyiv, where a Russian drone strike had destroyed a section of a five-storey residential building from the first to the fifth floor. Footage released by Ukraine’s State Emergency Service showed rescuers using an extended fire ladder and an aerial platform to help residents escape from the damaged structure, while other teams searched through piles of debris for possible survivors. According to Ukrainian authorities, nine residents, including one child, had been evacuated.
articles.body: Emergency workers rushed to the scene in Dymer, near Kyiv, where a Russian drone strike had destroyed a section of a five-storey residential building from the first to the fifth floor. Footage released by Ukraine’s State Emergency Service showed rescuers using an extended fire ladder and an aerial platform to help residents escape from the damaged structure, while other teams searched through piles of debris for possible survivors. According to Ukrainian authorities, nine residents, including one child, had been evacuated. The State Emergency Service initially said that up to seven people could be trapped beneath the rubble. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later said that 14 people were unaccounted for. The attack was part of a wider wave of Russian drone strikes reported across Ukraine overnight. Ukraine’s Air Force said 186 attack drones were launched, of which 161 were shot down. In Kharkiv, a strike drone hit the Kyivskyi district and started a fire. In Chernihiv, a Russian strike set a wood-processing plant ablaze, while in Zaporizhzhia three people, including two children, were injured in an evening attack. The extent of the destruction in Dymer raised fears for residents who might still be beneath the collapsed sections of the building. Rescue workers remained focused on removing debris and reaching potentially trapped people, with no confirmed outcome for those still missing at the time of the initial reports. The latest strikes once again exposed the dangers faced by civilians in residential areas as Russian aerial attacks continue across Ukraine.

articles.preview: Kraftwerk Berlin, part of same development as techno club Tresor, transformed into ‘war room’ for arms firm event With their cavernous post-industrial venues, teeth-grinding four-by-four beats and bouncers that look like Blade Runner extras, Berlin’s nightclubs trade on a reputation for bleakness. A recent event at one of the city’s most legendary clubland institutions, however, has proven too dystopian even for seasoned techno-heads.
articles.body:
With their cavernous post-industrial venues, teeth-grinding four-by-four beats and bouncers that look like Blade Runner extras, Berlin’s nightclubs trade on a reputation for bleakness. A recent event at one of the city’s most legendary clubland institutions, however, has proven too dystopian even for seasoned techno-heads.

On 11 November, the Kraftwerk Berlin arts complex had its central hall transformed into what visitors described as something resembling a war room, with maps and aerial footage projected on to concrete walls, drones hanging from the ceiling, and guards in flak jackets patrolling the premises with sniffer dogs.

Those who flocked to the venue – which hosts the experimental music festival Atonal and is part of the same complex as the techno club Tresor – had come for the launch of Clarity, an AI targeting system developed by the German arms startup Helsing.

Kraftwerk Berlin this week apologised for a “serious error of judgment” and vowed to revise its commercial rental department’s booking policy, after outrage over the event rippled through Berlin’s music scene. The row has raised uncomfortable questions about the commercialisation of the German capital’s famed nightlife, and the culture sector’s traditional pacifism at a time of growing security threats.

The Munich-based Helsing was founded in 2021 and counts the Swedish tech entrepreneur and Spotify co-founder Daniel Ek among its investors and board co-chairs. On its website, it describes Clarity as an agentic intelligence platform designed to use drone, satellite and sensor data to lock on to targets.

It claims that human operators remain responsible for approving any strikes.

Helsing says Clarity is “developed and built in Europe under European control”. The market leader for battlefield software is Palantir’s Maven, the system that has powered US military strikes on Iran this year. European governments have been scrambling for alternatives to US-developed systems. France’s domestic intelligence service has already announced it is dropping Palantir for a homegrown rival.

But European governments’ boosting of their arms industries is also clashing with an anti-militaristic cultural consensus – nowhere more so than in the former cold war pressure cooker of Berlin, where nightclubs became spaces to dance away the anxieties of the arms race.

“The fact there is a war in Europe and that Ukraine needs German support should not mean that we switch off all our critical faculties,” said Michail Stangl, a Berlin-based music curator and DJ. “We are already seeing how AI-driven targeting systems are being used in Gaza, and it’s hard to imagine that once a company like Helsing develops a successful arms system, it would not sell it on to authoritarian regimes, domestic police, or organisations like Frontex to be used against migrants.”

Speaking to the German broadcaster RBB at its launch event, a Helsing spokesperson said none of its military systems were designed to identify persons, and that Clarity was built to seek out objects such as radar systems, launch pads and ships.

It also said Clarity’s agents specialised in “looking for patterns of behaviour”, which could be interpreted as relating to human activity. Helsing did not respond to a request for comment.

The Clarity launch event was condemned in the strongest terms by Tresor, a nightclub and record label that acted as a bridge between post-Wall Berlin and Detroit’s electronic music scene in the 1990s. “It has no place in the spaces our community has built,” it said in a statement.

Tresor’s founder, the Berlin nightlife entrepreneur Dietmar-Maria “Dimitri” Hegemann, is also the managing director of Kraftwerk Berlin. Hegemann has called the booking “unacceptable”, saying it was done by “a staff member at the company responsible for Kraftwerk’s commercial rental business”, without him being consulted. Given his central role at the arts complex, and the level of planning usually required for such a high-security event, this has surprised some Berlin clubland insiders.

That Berlin’s former underground music venues are rented out for commercial purposes is no longer a deviation from the norm. As recently as 19 October, Kraftwerk Berlin hosted an investment summit organised by the German government and featuring a podium discussion between the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and the chip manufacturer Nvidia’s then chief executive, Jensen Huang.

In a Q&A released after the Clarity row, Kraftwerk Berlin said it had declined a proposed Palantir-sponsored event in 2022 after consulting its cultural teams.

Defenders of such commercial usages point out that many of Berlin’s nightclubs are struggling with rising rents and plummeting bar revenues. Kraftwerk Berlin may not be one of them, however. The total assets of its operating company, Schaltraum Berlin, were reported in June as having a value of €4.3m (£3.6m).
